Abstract: Synaptic dysfunction is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and proper localization of proteins involved in pre- and post-synaptic composition is dependent on endosomal recycling and trafficking, cellular processes involving the AD risk gene sortilin-related receptor 1 (SORL1). We examined SORL1's role in synaptic protein composition and neuronal function in human excitatory cortical neurons. Synaptic protein interactions were analyzed using a mesoscale proteomics assay. Immunocytochemistry was used to visualize synaptic proteins and α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor subunits. Neuronal function was measured with multi-electrode arrays. Loss of SORL1 expression significantly changes many synaptic protein-protein interactions and patterns of expression. SORL1-deficient neurons exhibit hyperactivity that is primarily amyloid beta independent. SORL1-deficient neurons also have impaired network plasticity. These findings further support a growing body of literature implicating early endosomal recycling defects as drivers of AD pathogenesis.
Authors: Williams CA; Rose SE; Stamenkovic V; Reid AN; Travaglini KJ; Smith SEP; Young JE
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Comorbidities and health-care use prior to early-onset Alzheimer's disease: A population-based case-control study.
Abstract: We examined whether comorbidities and health-care use differ between individuals later diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD) and matched controls during the 15 years preceding diagnosis. This population-based case-control study included 407 EOAD patients diagnosed at two Finnish university hospitals (2010-2021), and 4035 age- and sex-matched controls. Prior diagnoses and health-care visits were obtained from nationwide registers. EOAD patients had higher prevalence of vertigo (5.9% vs. 2.1%, p < 0.001), depression (5.7% vs. 2.3%, p < 0.001), headache (4.9% vs. 1.6%, p < 0.001), delirium (1.5% vs. 0.1%, p < 0.001), brain injuries (2.9% vs. 0.9%, p = 0.002), thyroid disorders (2.5% vs. 0.8%, p = 0.008), alcohol-related disorders (3.4% vs. 1.4%, p = 0.009), epilepsy (2.2% vs. 0.7%, p = 0.009), strokes (4.4% vs. 2.0%, p = 0.008), and otorhinolaryngologic diseases (5.2% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.027) 1-5 years before diagnosis. Only otorhinolaryngologic diseases (4.7% vs. 2.1%, p = 0.036) differed 6 to 10 years prior, whereas no differences were seen 11 to 15 years before diagnosis. Hypertension and dyslipidemia showed no between-group differences. Health-care use increased markedly from year before EOAD diagnosis. EOAD is preceded by recognizable patterns of morbidity and increased health-care use, which may support earlier detection.
Authors: Leppänen L; Lehtonen A; Aaltonen M; Aho K; Kivisild A; Ullgren A; Rinnankoski I; Soppela H; Haapasalo A; Portaankorva AM; Hartikainen P; Katisko K; Solje E; Krüger J
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Dysregulated mRNA Translation in Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Opportunities, and Challenges for Clinical Translation.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder and a growing public health concern. Its core pathological features include cerebral amyloid-β deposition and tau aggregation. mRNA translation is a tightly regulated process essential for gene expression and protein synthesis. It plays critical roles in neural development, synaptogenesis, and synaptic plasticity. In recent years, dysregulated translational control has been recognized as an important pathogenic mechanism in several neurological diseases, including AD. This review provides an integrated overview of the biological basis and mechanisms of dysregulated mRNA translation in AD, including translation initiation and elongation, local synaptic translation, abnormalities in RNA-binding proteins and stress granules, tRNA dysregulation, and the effects of AD-related genetic factors on translational control. Beyond the classic mechanisms of protein aggregation, the onset and progression of AD are also accompanied by abnormal translational regulation, involving initiation, elongation, and local synaptic translation. A major feature of these abnormalities is the coexistence of suppressed global protein synthesis and selectively enhanced translation of certain disease-related mRNAs, involving the integrated stress response, eIF2α/eIF4E signaling, eEF2K/eEF2 pathway, and RNA-binding protein dysfunction. Translational dysregulation provides a new perspective for understanding the molecular pathology of AD and has prompted the exploration of interventions targeting key nodes in translational control. Strategies targeting the integrated stress response, cap-dependent translation initiation, eEF2K, and tau-RNA-binding protein interactions have shown potential to improve synaptic function and cognitive phenotypes in animal models, although their safety and clinical translatability require further evaluation. This review provides an up-to-date reference for understanding translation-centered mechanisms in AD and evaluating emerging therapeutic strategies targeting translational control.
Authors: Li L; Dai F; Liu H; He S; Zhang X; Tao QQ

Title: Direction-specific biomarker profiles and clinical significance of plasma p-tau217/amyloid PET discordance in cognitively normal adults.
Abstract: Plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau)217 is increasingly used to triage amyloid testing, but the biological and clinical meaning of discordant plasma p-tau217 and amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) results in cognitively normal adults remains uncertain. We analyzed cognitively normal participants from the Chinese Preclinical Alzheimer's Disease Study (CPAS; n = 594) and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; n = 475). Amyloid PET positivity was defined as Centiloid ≥ 20. Cohort-specific p-tau217 positivity was defined using PET-anchored cutoffs with ≥ 0.90 specificity, yielding four p-tau/PET groups. Linear models assessed cross-sectional biomarker and cognitive differences; mixed-effects and Cox models assessed ADNI longitudinal Centiloid accumulation, cognitive trajectories, and clinical progression. In cross-sectional analyses, compared to p-tau-/PET-, p-tau+/PET- had higher glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels across cohorts; p-tau-/PET+ showed a lower plasma amyloid beta 42/40 ratio in ADNI; and p-tau+/PET+ showed the broadest multimodal abnormalities. In ADNI, both p-tau+ groups had higher clinical progression risk and faster decline in selected cognitive domains; both PET+ groups showed faster Centiloid accumulation. Faster Centiloid accumulation in p-tau+/PET- was observed only at lower specificity thresholds. Discordant plasma p-tau217 and amyloid PET results should be interpreted according to both the positivity pattern and the p-tau217 cutoff applied. Distinguishing these patterns may aid risk stratification and longitudinal monitoring. Different p-tau217 operating points may support risk enrichment and prioritization for confirmatory amyloid testing, but require validation before clinical use.
Authors: Huang Y; Huang L; Cui L; Pan F; Xie F; Guo H; Guo Q
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Surface proteins modulate extracellular vesicle mediated inhibition of Aβ(1-42) aggregation.
Abstract: Aggregation of the amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide into amyloid oligomers and fibrils is a central pathogenic feature and therapeutic target in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Understanding the aggregation reaction and how it is modulated by the biological environment is therefore important. Cell-secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs) are emerging as modulators of Aβ aggregation, transport and toxicity. Here, we show that EVs from a variety of human and non-human cells have highly similar retarding effects on the rate of Aβ(1-42) fibril formation, suggesting that aggregation inhibition is a common EV feature. Furthermore, we examine how different EV biomolecular classes contribute to shape this effect. We show that enzymatic removal of surface-associated EV proteins significantly enhances their ability to inhibit aggregation. Similar, albeit considerably smaller, alterations were observed upon removal of cell surface protein-associated glycans. This suggests that EV-mediated inhibition of Aβ(1-42) aggregation may primarily be regulated by lipids and that surface proteins function to modulate this effect, through steric hindrance and/or direct interactions with Aβ(1-42) species. We further observed a minor but statistically robust enhancement of EV-mediated Aβ(1-42) aggregation inhibition upon removal of proteoglycans, suggesting that carbohydrates on the EV-surface also contribute to modulate their inhibitory effect. Altogether, these observations contribute mechanistic insight into the role of EVs as modulators of Aβ aggregation and highlight their possible contributions to maintenance of extracellular protein homeostasis.
Authors: Halipi V; Daoutsali G; Havemeister F; de Carvalho V; Görgens A; El Andaloussi S; Esbjörner EK
Journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society

Title: Rationally Designed Peptides and Peptoids as Inhibitors of Amyloid-β (Aβ) Aggregation.
Abstract: Peptide and peptoid are two types of peptidomimetics can be used as drugs for diseases. One of the main hallmarks in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is Aβ aggregation. Due to the natural affinity between peptide and Aβ proteins, peptide therapeutics are found out to be suitable for the disease, as they are almost nontoxic, possess good biocompatibility and are structurally changeable. This review mainly focuses on peptide and peptoid as inhibitors targeting Aβ protein, elaborating on their design strategies and some of their inhibitory effects, providing diverse potential compounds for the treatment of AD. The involved peptide inhibitors are classified into three major categories based on their structural features: inhibitors based on the natural Aβ sequence, inhibitors based on non-natural Aβ sequences, and inhibitors conjugated with small molecule compounds. To facilitate understanding of the development process of each type of inhibitor, we have expounded on each major category in terms of chronological order, specialty and importance. It also summarized the challenges and design strategies faced by peptide inhibitors in targeting Aβ aggregation. This review provides a valuable resource for researchers in the field of synthetic peptide and their biomedical applications, offering structural insights into the design of new peptide for better diagnosis and therapeutic applications.
Authors: Huang X; Ma S; Li X; Pan J

Title: Dietary Patterns, Micronutrient Adequacy, and Metabolic Vulnerability in Alzheimer's Disease: A Critical Narrative Review.
Abstract: Dietary factors may influence cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD), but observational associations, mechanistic findings, and intervention effects should not be considered equivalent evidence. This critical narrative review examines how dietary patterns, micronutrient adequacy, and metabolic health may modify AD-related vulnerability. A targeted search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science through April 2026 prioritized systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized trials, and prospective cohorts. Mediterranean, Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND), and healthful plant-based dietary patterns have been associated with better cognitive outcomes and lower dementia risk. However, evidence remains predominantly observational, and randomized trials have not consistently demonstrated prevention of cognitive decline. Strict vegan diets have not shown additional protection beyond high-quality plant-based diets and require careful attention to vitamin B12 and overall nutritional adequacy. Ketogenic diets and medium-chain triglycerides may increase cerebral ketone availability, but their cognitive benefits remain inconsistent, and disease modification has not been established. Although vitamin B12, folate, and vitamin D support neural and metabolic functions, correcting deficiency should not be equated with treating AD. Overall, nutrition should be viewed as a contributor to cardiometabolic and neurological resilience and as part of person-centered dementia care, rather than as a stand-alone disease-modifying therapy. Future studies should integrate accurate dietary assessment, objective adherence measures, metabolic phenotyping, AD biomarkers, and clinically meaningful outcomes.
Authors: Sierralta I; Pinilla M; Servili E; Ormazabal P; Bastías-Pérez M; Cisternas P; Inestrosa NC

Title: Network-dependent remote effects and local tau burden jointly shape neuronal dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD) propagates along the brain's connectome, yet the mechanisms by which tau drives neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. We hypothesized that dysfunction primarily emerges in regions close to tau-harboring epicenters. One hundred thirty-one amyloid-positive individuals underwent dynamic [<sup>18</sup>F]PI-2620 tau positron emission tomography. Kinetic modeling yielded distribution volume ratios (DVRs) and perfusion (R1). Tau epicenters were defined as top 10% DVR regions. Connectivity-based distance to epicenters was derived from normative resting-state functional connectivity. At the individual level, hypoperfusion was more closely related to distance from tau epicenters than to local tau deposition, particularly in early AD, consistent with diaschisis-like disconnection. With advancing biological disease severity, local tau deposition increasingly converged with hypoperfusion. Critically, hypoperfusion mediated the relationship between tau accumulation and cognitive decline. Tau epicenters shape the brain-wide pattern of neuronal dysfunction, while local tau burden determines the degree of damage driving cognitive decline.
Authors: Frontzkowski L; Roemer-Cassiano S; Gnörich J; Janowitz D; Eyob H; Probst K; Dhoqina D; Dewenter A; Steward A; Zhu Z; Klonowski M; Hirsch F; Biel D; Paulus M; Vöglein J; Schönecker S; Rauchmann BS; Kurz C; Koriath C; Häckert J; Stöcklein S; Palleis C; Perneczky R; Levin J; Buerger K; Werner RA; Höglinger G; Brendel M; Franzmeier N
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Exercise promotes lipophagy and mitigates cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease through downregulating microglial TMEM9.
Abstract: Autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction contributes to lipid droplet (LD) accumulation, which drives pathological progression in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Exercise is reported to restore autophagy-lysosomal function and attenuate cognitive impairment in AD, but its regulation of LD deposition remains unknown. 5×FAD transgenic mice underwent a three-month exercise intervention. Cognitive and emotional behaviors were assessed using the Morris water maze, novel object recognition, and open field test. LD deposition was evaluated by oil red O and BODIPY staining. Proteomic sequencing was performed to identify proteins affected by exercise. Pathological changes were examined by immunofluorescence, western blotting, and transmission electron microscopy. Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV was used to overexpress or knock down microglial TMEM9 to investigate the mechanisms by which physical exercise affects behavior and pathology in AD. In vitro, BV2 cells were cultured and incubated with oligomeric amyloid-β (oAβ), with or without oleic acid to induce LD formation. Chloroquine and rapamycin, which regulate autophagy-lysosomal function, were used to examine the effects of LDs on mitochondrial integrity under glucose deprivation conditions. Lentiviral or plasmid transfection was used to explore the key role of TMEM9 in regulating lipophagy, and the interaction between TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 was detected by co-immunoprecipitation. Clinically, plasma TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 levels in AD patients were measured by ELISA, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate diagnostic performance. Exercise mitigated cerebral LD deposition through enhanced lipophagy, preserving mitochondrial integrity and attenuating cognitive decline. Mechanistically, exercise suppressed microglial TMEM9 expression, restoring LD degradation. Tmem9 downregulation facilitated LKB1 lysosomal translocation, activating AMPK signaling. In vitro, oleic acid-induced LDs preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and increased ATP production in BV2 microglia under glucose deprivation and oAβ exposure. Tmem9 overexpression exacerbated lipophagy impairment and mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas Tmem9 knockdown enhanced lipophagy and cytoprotection. Aβ clearance was negatively regulated by TMEM9. Clinically, AD patients exhibited characteristic Aβ deposition and glucose hypometabolism, with plasma TMEM9 levels strongly correlating with p-tau217 progression. Plasma TMEM9 and the TMEM9/ATP6AP1 ratio emerged as potential AD diagnostic biomarkers (AUC=0.791 and 0.853, respectively). These findings establish exercise-induced TMEM9 inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy targeting lipidostasis to combat AD progression.
Authors: Zhang L; Li S; Ma X; Cheng S; Ye Z; Liu S; Qin L; Dong H; Feng Y; Li M; Xu J; Cai L; Hu X; He X

Title: ELDER MISTREATMENT: A ROAD TO A NEW RISK ALGORITHM USING ICD-10 DATA.
Abstract: Elder mistreatment (EM)-a growing public health problem in the United States-is associated with poor quality of life, accelerated disability, and premature death. EM remains underrecognized and underreported, with the diagnosis frequently being made at a late stage when the afflicted older adults have experienced prolonged suffering including emotional, physical, and financial abuse. One way to increase early EM recognition and timely management is through the development and implementation of predictive algorithms that can help alert clinicians to the need for additional screening. In earlier work, using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) diagnostics codes, we were able to develop a logistic regression approach to determine an EM predictive algorithm with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.73, a sensitivity of 80%, and specificity of 47%. Subsequently, this model was applied to a vulnerable group of older adults-those with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). In this cohort, we found illiteracy to be the strongest predictor associated with EM. These EM predictive algorithms can be useful in the creation of electronic health record (EHR) reminders to prompt clinicians to suspect EM and implement appropriate follow-up care plans.
Authors: Mouton CP; Pappadis M; Schlag K; Westra J; Kuo YF; Raji M; Wood L; Temple J
Journal: Transactions of the American Clinical and Climatological Association

Title: Noninvasive ultrashort wave neuromodulation enhances glymphatic clearance to alleviate traumatic brain edema and Alzheimer's pathology.
Abstract: The glymphatic system clears cerebral waste, yet strategies to enhance its function remain elusive. Here, we show that 40.68 MHz ultrashort wave (USW) rapidly enhances glymphatic bulk flow in healthy mice within 10 minutes. USW potentiates both glymphatic influx and efflux, concomitant with increased Delta wave neuronal synchronization, as confirmed by local field potentials and electroencephalograms. Chemogenetic silencing confirms that USW-driven glymphatic enhancement depends on neuronal activity, while pharmacological blockade of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) abolishes the effects, revealing dual reliance on neural dynamics and astrocytic water channels. Mechanistically, USW-induced Delta oscillations promote AQP4 polarization, coupling synchronized firing to perivascular AQP4 redistribution. Moreover, USW ameliorates traumatic brain injury-induced cerebral edema and improves cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's mice by restoring glymphatic function. Our findings establish USW as a non-invasive neuromodulatory strategy for enhancing glymphatic clearance, offering therapeutic potential for neurological disorders characterized by glymphatic dysfunction.
Authors: Liu J; Xu C; Ruan H; Zhang K; Wang F; Qin Q; Li X; Chen Y; Tan Y; Qiu Y; Chen H; Wang Y; Yang Z; Zhang Y; Zhu Y; Chang C; Jiang X; Peng N

Title: Characterizing hippocampal activation during pattern separation with multi-echo fMRI in cognitively normal older adults.
Abstract: Hippocampal hyperactivity, detected with mnemonic similarity task (MST) fMRI, is both a promising marker of risk and a probable driver of degeneration in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, implementation of such fMRI in interventional research is limited by long scan times and the absence of a framework for identifying prospective participants with hyperactivity who could be targeted with therapeutic approaches aimed at reducing this activity. We used multi-echo fMRI during the MST, an episodic memory task previously shown to engage hippocampal subfields CA3 and dentate gyrus (DG), to characterize activity profiles in 33 cognitively normal older adults. We compared MST-related CA3 and DG activation and behavioural performance across subsets of eight task runs. Behavioural and activation effects were equivalent for the first set of four runs (Runs-A) and the second set (Runs-B), suggesting that robust data can be obtained with four runs. Left and right CA3 + DG activation did not differ. We provide an exemplar framework for the derivation of a threshold for single-participant classification of elevated hippocampal activation as an indicator of AD risk in cognitively normal older individuals. Scalable (~22 min) multi-echo MST fMRI robustly captures hippocampal activation and provides a framework for individual-level characterization of hippocampal function in cognitively normal older adults. This enables individualized detection of elevated hippocampal activation as a modifiable risk factor and may guide enrolment into prevention trials targeting preclinical AD.
Authors: Solar KG; Kashyap S; Deom N; Uludağ K; Zotovic L; Lanctôt K; Black SE; McAndrews MP

Title: Quantitative analysis of intersecting pentagon drawings for interpretable cognitive impairment screening.
Abstract: BackgroundThe intersecting pentagon drawing task in the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), also referred to as the Pentagon Drawing Test (PDT), is a brief cognitive screening tool in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other cognitive disorders. However, conventional manual scoring is coarse and may overlook clinically meaningful variation in drawing performance.ObjectiveTo evaluate whether quantitative PDT features can support interpretable screening for cognitive impairment.MethodsWe analyzed participants who completed the MMSE, Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and PDT. Cognitive impairment was defined using education-adjusted MMSE and MoCA cutoffs. Eight quantitative drawing features characterized geometric integrity, spatial organization, and graphomotor characteristics. These features, together with demographic variables, were evaluated for prediction of a modified MMSE-derived cognitive score and classification of cognitive status using cross-validation.ResultsA total of 3478 participants were included, including 2463 with cognitive impairment and 1015 cognitively normal individuals. All eight quantitative drawing features were significantly lower in the cognitive impairment group. Shape regularity, vertices, alignment and intersection area proportion showed the strongest positive correlations with modified MMSE scores. The model achieved an R<sup>2</sup> of 0.42 for score prediction and showed a positive correlation between predicted and observed scores (Spearman ρ = 0.64). For cognitive impairment classification, the model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.832, sensitivity of 82.5%, specificity of 67.4%, PPV of 86.0%, NPV of 61.4%, and F1-score of 0.842.ConclusionsQuantitative features of PDT showed interpretable associations with cognitive screening outcomes. This approach may support scalable and objective cognitive screening and serve as a complement to clinical assessment.
Authors: Xing R; Sun W; Zhou J; Chen T; Chen L; Peng P; Xu G

Title: Systemic oxidative stress in patients with Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder and oxidative stress (OS) is believed to play a role in disease pathogenesis. However, reliable OS markers are lacking. In this study we aim to assess OS in AD by evaluating free thiols, which serve as key indicators of the systemic redox status. SCD (subjective cognitive decline), MCI (mild cognitive impairment), AD, and other dementias (Non-AD) were recruited. Comorbidity data were collected and free thiols were measured in plasma. Additionally, phosphorylated-Tau (pTau217), amyloid-beta ratio (Aβ42/40), Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP), and neurofilament light (NfL) levels were used to investigate correlation with free thiols. Further, associations between free thiols and disease severity in AD were calculated. Three hundred and ten patients were included (SCD 109, MCI 51, AD 125, Non-AD 25). Free thiols were significantly lower in AD compared to SCD and MCI (p < 0.01). Free thiols correlated negatively with pTau217, NfL and GFAP, also within AD (p < 0.01 for all). Additionally, free thiols significantly negatively correlated with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) scores (N = 210, p < 0.001). Multiple linear regression showed that type 2 diabetes and age were significant predictors for free thiols (B = 1.01, β = 0.266, p < 0.001; B = -0.040, β = -0.273, p < 0.001, respectively). After adjusting for these covariates, free thiols remained significantly lower in AD compared to SCD (p < 0.05). Increased systemic OS, reflected by lower free thiols, is observed in plasma of AD patients, supporting a key role for OS in AD-pathophysiology and highlighting free thiols as potential therapeutic targets and possibly complementary biomarkers for clinical diagnostics.
Authors: Verwey NA; Kloppenburg-Lagendijk M; Bulthuis MLC; Ferket W; Koning AM; van Goor H; Bourgonje AR

Title: Clinical Factors Associated With Discordant Plasma P-Tau217 and Established Alzheimer Disease Biomarkers.
Abstract: Plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau) 217 is increasingly used for Alzheimer disease (AD) diagnosis and treatment decisions but may be discordant with established AD biomarkers. False-positive (FP) plasma results may lead to overtreatment and false-negative (FN) results to missed or delayed disease-modifying therapies. We evaluated factors associated with discordant results. This retrospective study included participants enrolled in memory and aging studies at Mayo Clinic with "positive" (>0.324 pg/mL) or "negative" (<0.186 pg/mL) plasma p-tau217 results and confirmatory AD biomarkers. Plasma results were classified as true positive (TP), true negative (TN), FP, or FN, referencing amyloid-PET and CSF p-tau181/β-amyloid (Aβ) 42. Clinical and laboratory variables were compared using univariate analyses; multivariable logistic regression evaluated independent associations with discordance. Among 706 participants (median 70.0 [interquartile range 15.8] years; 54% male), 60 (8.5%) had discordant plasma p-tau217 results. FN results (5.6%) were more frequent than FP results (2.8%; p = 0.007). Discordance was associated with older age (odds ratio [OR] 1.61 per decade, 95% CI 1.23-2.14) and obstructive sleep apnea (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.08-3.49). FN (vs TP) results were associated with milder clinical stage (global Clinical Dementia Rating [CDR] ≤0.5 vs CDR ≥1; p < 0.001), higher Mini-Mental State Examination scores (OR 1.20 per point, 95% CI 1.05-1.36), obstructive sleep apnea (OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.01-4.3), higher body mass index (OR 1.11/kg/m2, 95% CI 1.03-1.20), and higher estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR: OR 1.33/10 mL/min/1.73 m2, 95% CI 1.05-1.69). In age-adjusted models, body mass index (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.25), eGFR (OR 1.63/10 mL/min/1.73 m2, 95% CI 1.22-2.16), and earlier clinical stage (CDR ≤0.5) were independently associated with FN results. FP (vs TN) results were associated with older age (OR 2.37, 95% CI 1.36-4.09), thyroid disease (OR 4.41, 95% CI 1.36-14.3), lower eGFR (OR 0.48/10 mL/min/1.73 m2, 95% CI 0.31-0.66), and advanced disease stage (CDR ≥1). In age-adjusted models, eGFR (OR 0.54/10 mL/min/1.73 m2, 95% CI 0.35-0.82) and advanced disease stage (CDR ≥ 1 vs CDR 0: OR 11.11, 95% CI 2.0-50.0; vs CDR 0.5: OR 4.55, 95% CI 1.12-16.67) were independently associated with FP results. Plasma p-tau217 results and established AD biomarkers were discordant in 8.5% of participants. Clinical stage and factors related to brain amyloid clearance, renal clearance, and volume of distribution were associated with discordant results. These insights may inform mechanisms of discordance and identify patients requiring confirmatory biomarker measures.
Authors: Shir D; Algeciras-Schimnich A; Piura YD; Bornhorst JA; Figdore DJ; Elgenidi A; Lachner C; Graff-Radford NR; Day GS

Title: Histone Modifications at the Intersection of Aging, Neuroinflammation and Metabolism in Alzheimer's Disease.
Abstract: Aging, neuroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction are tightly intertwined in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but how transient pathological signals become persistent cellular states remains poorly understood. Histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) provide a dynamic interface between extracellular stimuli, cellular metabolism and chromatin state. This Review examines how canonical histone modifications and emerging metabolite-derived acylations regulate inflammatory and stress-responsive programmes across microglia, astrocytes and neurons during aging and AD. We discuss how amyloid-β, tau pathology, metabolic dysfunction and innate immune signaling converge on histone-modifying machinery, and how reciprocal interactions between metabolism and chromatin may stabilize disease-associated cell states. Particular attention is given to cellular senescence and neuroimmune memory, while emphasizing the context dependence of individual histone marks across cell types, genomic regions and disease stages. We further evaluate evidence for causality using three criteria: perturbation, persistence and reversibility. This framework distinguishes chromatin states that accompany ongoing pathology from those capable of sustaining pathological cell states beyond their initiating signals. Finally, we consider therapeutic strategies targeting histone-modifying enzymes, chromatin readers and metabolic inputs to restore chromatin plasticity and promote resolution of chronic neuroinflammation.
Authors: Liang J; Cao H; Ren X; Sha N; Han X; Jiang L; Liu B; Zhao W

Title: Achieving detailed medial temporal lobe segmentation with upsampled isotropic training from implicit neural representation.
Abstract: Imaging biomarkers in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are important tools for diagnosing, tracking and treating Alzheimer's disease (AD). Neurofibrillary tau pathology in AD is closely linked to neurodegeneration and generally follows a pattern of spread in the brain, with early stages involving subregions of the medial temporal lobe (MTL). Accurate segmentation of MTL subregions is needed to extract granular biomarkers of AD progression. MTL subregions are often imaged using T2-weighted (T2w) MRI scans that are highly anisotropic due to constraints of MRI physics and image acquisition, making it difficult to reliably model MTL subregions geometrically and extract morphological measures, such as thickness. In this study, we propose a segmentation framework for MTL subregions in isotropic space, in which an implicit neural representation is used to construct the isotropic training atlas from the anisotropic low-resolution T2w data, with T1w MRI as an auxiliary modality to support the INR and segmentation. In an independent test set, the morphological measures extracted using this isotropic model showed stronger effect sizes than those from models trained on anisotropic data in distinguishing participants with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from cognitively unimpaired individuals. In the test-retest analysis, the morphological measures extracted using the isotropic model showed greater stability than those from the anisotropic segmentation. This study demonstrates improved reliability of MRI-derived MTL subregion biomarkers without additional atlas annotation effort, which may more accurately quantify and track the relationship between AD pathology and brain atrophy for monitoring disease progression.
Authors: Li Y; Khandelwal P; Jena R; Xie L; Duong MT; Denning AE; Brown CA; Wisse LEM; Das SR; Wolk DA; Yushkevich PA

Title: Amyloid-Induced Network Resilience and Collapse in Alzheimer's Disease: Insights From Computational Modeling.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease is marked by progressive synaptic loss and cognitive decline, with amyloid-beta accumulation playing a central pathological role. Although the molecular effects of amyloid-beta are well-characterized, the cascade from local synaptic dysfunction to large-scale network collapse remains poorly understood. We present a biophysically grounded computational model that integrates small-world network topology, Izhikevich neuron dynamics, short-term plasticity, and amyloid-beta-induced synaptic pruning to investigate how amyloid burden degrades functional brain connectivity over time. Crucially, we simulate the evolving network dynamics across disease stages, revealing how firing rate, synchrony, variability, and Fano factor evolve in response to progressive structural degradation. Our results demonstrate a two-phase deterioration: Initial compensatory dynamics followed by abrupt disintegration of coordinated activity. This temporal dissociation mirrors clinical observations and offers mechanistic insight into Alzheimer's disease progression. We further identify a critical accumulated amyloid dose beyond which network collapse becomes inevitable, preceded by early-warning indicators such as declining global efficiency and the spectral radius of the network connections. Network topology, synaptic time constants, and repair mechanisms strongly influence resilience, with small-world networks showing delayed collapse and greater functional compensation. Finite-size scaling reveals that larger networks experience earlier and sharper phase transitions. Ultimately, by establishing a mathematical link between microscopic synaptic degradation and macroscopic network failure, our findings suggest that if experimental proxies for the spectral radius can be identified, they would serve as highly sensitive early-warning indicators of impending network collapse. This theoretical framework offers new mechanistic targets for the early detection and therapeutic monitoring of neurodegenerative diseases.
Authors: Nguessap ELF; Depannemaecker D; Ferreira FF

Title: Cannabidiol in Alzheimer's disease: evidence-weighted molecular mechanisms and translational challenges.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex, progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which amyloid-β accumulation, tau dysregulation, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, synaptic loss and neurodegeneration interact to drive memory loss and cognitive decline. Despite advances in symptomatic therapies and anti-amyloid agents, clinical benefit remains modest, supporting interest in polypharmacological approaches. Cannabidiol (CBD) is a non-psychotropic phytocannabinoid that interacts with several signalling systems relevant to AD, including cannabinoid-related pathways, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ), transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channels, 5-HT1A signalling, fatty acid-binding proteins involved in anandamide transport, GPR55 and adenosine transporters. The most consistent preclinical findings indicate that CBD attenuates neuroinflammatory and oxidative responses and improves selected behavioural outcomes. Evidence for amyloid-related effects is supportive but heterogeneous. Direct evidence for tau modulation has expanded in transgenic and chemically induced models, but findings remain model-dependent, whereas mitochondrial rescue and adult hippocampal neurogenesis are less firmly established. Methodological variability in CBD source, formulation, dose, route, treatment window, sex, age and outcome selection limits direct comparison between studies. Work on other cannabinoids and CBD:Δ9-THC combinations is discussed for context, and current evidence does not establish CBD as a disease-modifying treatment in AD. Overall, current preclinical evidence supports continued investigation of CBD as a multi-target neuroprotective candidate in AD, provided that future studies use standardized, mechanism-focused and translationally relevant designs. This review compares preclinical evidence across pathological domains and identifies translational research priorities.
Authors: Sura S; Jagadeesan S; Masrudin SS; Moklas MAM; Nor NHM

Title: Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
Abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain-periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer's disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.
Authors: Shi H; Zhao Y; Zhu W; Wang YJ; Bu XL

Title: Spatiotemporal heterogeneity and dynamic evolution of microglial glucose metabolic reprogramming in Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is accompanied by persistent disturbances in brain energy metabolism, and microglial glucose metabolic reprogramming constitutes an important link among pathological protein deposition, neuroinflammation, and impaired clearance. This review examines these metabolic changes across disease stages, brain regions, and plaque-associated microenvironments and proposes a dynamic state-composition model. In this model, microglia in different metabolic states coexist, and their relative proportions and spatial distribution change as AD progresses. In early disease or during active phagocytosis, some microglia show enhanced glycolytic and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) programs. Under persistent pathological stress, increased glucose uptake may not translate into effective energy production and can coexist with inflammation and impaired lipid metabolism. In late disease, microglia with reduced metabolic capacity and impaired phagocytosis become more prevalent. However, higher expression of OXPHOS-related genes in some microglial states associated with tau pathology does not necessarily indicate improved mitochondrial respiration. These population-level patterns do not imply that individual microglia follow a fixed sequence of metabolic changes. Longitudinal cell tracking and microglia-specific metabolic flux measurements are needed to test this model and inform interventions tailored to disease stage and microglial state.
Authors: Chen Y; Li F; Zhang J; Wei M; Ni J; Li T; Yao L; Tian J; Shi J
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Guardians at the gate: cMAF keeps the brain's vasculature in check.
Abstract: In this issue of Cell, Brioschi et al. identify cellular musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma (cMAF) as a key regulator of brain perivascular macrophages that supports cerebrovascular function through insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) production. This cMAF-IGF1 program is enhanced in Alzheimer's disease (AD), potentially reflecting a protective response that is lost in APOE4 carriers.
Authors: Alexopoulou L; Rua R

Title: Plasma eMTBR-tau243 as a disease biomarker across Alzheimer's disease clinical phenotypes.
Abstract: The concentration of endogenous tau microtubule-binding region containing residue-243 in plasma (eMTBR-tau243) has been proposed to be a sensitive biomarker of tangle pathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD). We assessed eMTBR-tau243 and phosphorylated tau217 (p-tau217) with tau and Aβ-positron emission tomography (PET) across different AD clinical phenotypes. Plasma eMTBR-tau243, p-tau217, and the ratio of non-phosphorylated to phosphorylated tau217 (%p-tau217) were measured in 20 Aβ-PET positive AD patients representing four clinical phenotypes and 10 cognitively unimpaired controls. Plasma levels were correlated with PET, demographic and cognitive variables. Plasma eMTBR-tau243, p-tau217, and %p-tau217 levels were greater in AD than controls, with greatest levels observed in motor-predominant AD. Plasma biomarker levels correlated with cortical flortaucipir-PET uptake; eMTBR-tau243 correlations were strongest. In AD, eMTBR-tau243 levels were undetectable in patients with mild/focal flortaucipir-PET uptake (45%). Only eMTBR-tau243 correlated with cognition. Plasma eMTBR-tau243 may be an excellent biomarker for tau deposition and cognition in AD across different phenotypes.
Authors: Whitwell JL; Bhaskaran JG; Satoh R; Graff-Radford J; Machulda MM; Lowe VJ; Mielke MM; Dickson DW; Tzeng SC; Bui J; Verghese PB; West T; Venkatesh V; Josephs KA
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Natural Products Targeting Alzheimer's Disease via NF-κB Pathway: A Review.
Abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a severe neurological condition marked by cognitive decline and memory loss, affecting millions worldwide. Current therapeutic approaches for AD are primarily palliative, have slight effectiveness in arresting disease progression, and are frequently associated with significant adverse effects. In light of these limitations, there is a growing interest in exploring alternative medicinal strategies centred on phytogenic natural compounds. The nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway is a critical biological target, essential for regulating the inflammatory response associated with the advancement of AD. Targeting the NF-κB signalling system is a promising approach for alleviating neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, although it operates in coordination with other pathways such as Nrf2 and MAPK, which also play significant roles in the complex pathophysiology of AD. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the current studies about natural compounds and their potential therapeutic effects in AD, emphasising compounds obtained from various plant sources. We examine the mechanisms regulating the NF-κB pathway through the analysis of preclinical studies, evaluating its efficacy in reducing neurodegeneration and improving cognitive function in AD patients. Furthermore, future directions and conclusions have been incorporated, which jointly emphasise the significance of phytochemicals in modifying NF-κB and the associated signalling processes.
Authors: Hasan F; Thippamma K; Kumar V; Baiseitova A; Ikram M; Shah AB

Title: Synthetic Insights on Donepezil: An Anti-Alzheimer Drug.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease is a severe condition that poses significant global health concerns to international health agencies and remains a major threat to public health. As there is no cure for Alzheimer's disease, various anti-Alzheimer's medications are used to manage its symptoms. Donepezil is one of the most highly marketed drugs, known for its positive effects on cognition, function, behaviour and overall patient condition, making it a standout treatment option. Various synthetic methods have been developed to produce more efficient pathways that minimise by-products and maximise yield. This review summarises the reported literature on various synthetic routes for producing Donepezil. We have also made an effort to highlight the advantages and limitations of prior literature, which may lead to potential improvements for future research. This work will serve as a foundation for upcoming researchers, ultimately benefiting the well-being of Alzheimer's patients and human society as a whole.
Authors: Khuman YM; Kapadiya YM; Maru JJ

Title: Amyloid PET is a cost-effective exam to monitor Donanemab treatment in Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies are the first drugs approved as disease targeted therapies for the treatment of early Alzheimer's disease (AD). Donanemab and Lecanemab have shown a reduction of amyloid in amyloid PET scans, with an average of - 55.48 centiloids in the Lecanemab trial and - 88.0 centiloids in the Donanemab trial at 18 months. Despite their efficacy, these treatments are associated with amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), necessitating regular MRI surveillance and strategies that minimize treatment duration to reduce risk. Economic modeling indicates that amyloid PET at 52 weeks is cost-effective when its cost is below 20.8-23.2% of the price of 78-week Donanemab therapy, translating into substantial savings and reduced adverse-event exposure. Studies with lecanemab are missing. Broader implementation is limited by access, cost, and the need for standardized centiloid quantification. Overall, amyloid PET appears to be a valuable tool for guiding duration-limited Donanemab therapy and may improve safety, efficiency, and resource utilization.
Authors: Tábuas-Pereira M; Moreira AP; Castelo-Branco M; Abrunhosa A; Santana I
Journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

Title: Hemicyanine-Based Wash-Free Near-Infrared Fluorescent Probe for Imaging Amyloid-β Aggregates in Alzheimer's Disease.
Abstract: As a key biomarker of Alzheimer's disease (AD), amyloid-β (Aβ) is frequently employed for the diagnosis of AD. Near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) imaging is a non-invasive, low-cost route for visualizing Aβ in vivo. However, most existing Aβ NIRF probes require tedious washing steps, show modest fluorescence turn-on (<50-fold), and stain normal tissue non-specifically. In this work, by fine-tuning the amphiphilicity of a hemicyanine scaffold to place its log P within the appropriate range, we identified P3 as a wash-free NIRF probe for Aβ aggregates. P3 bound Aβ aggregates with high affinity. In vivo, P3 distinguished AD mice from wild-type mice with a 4.8-fold signal ratio, together with adequate brain uptake (1.5 ± 0.1 ID/g at 20 min) and rapid clearance. Unlike Thioflavin T, which indiscriminately labels Aβ aggregates and normal neurons, P3 specifically labeled Aβ aggregates with negligible background, which enabled wash-free imaging with a signal-to-noise ratio of 80 ± 4. This work provides a wash-free, high-affinity NIRF probe for Aβ imaging.
Authors: Zhao X; Liang R; Li Y; Yan J; Zhang J; Su Z; Liu Y; Yang H; Cheng M

Title: Association of Nut Consumption with Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease.
Abstract: Background: Nut consumption reduces risks of cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease and depression. However, its association with dementia and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains unclear. Methods: A population-based case-control study was conducted in China, including 466 participants aged 52-100 years (233 with dementia). Data on socio-demographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, and dietary intake over the past two years were collected through structured face-to-face interviews. Nut consumption was categorised as non-consumption or Results: Of the 466 participants, 59.0% reported consuming nuts at non-consumption or Conclusions: Higher nut consumption was associated with reduced risks of dementia and AD. Increasing nut intake may represent a potential strategy for dementia and AD prevention. However, large-scale cohort and interventional studies are needed to further clarify the association and determine the magnitude of the effect.
Authors: Chen R

Title: The Interplay Between Oophorectomy and Alzheimer's Disease: A Narrative Review.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia worldwide and affects women more frequently than men. Although age remains the main risk factor, reproductive aging and changes in ovarian hormone exposure may also contribute to this difference. Premenopausal bilateral oophorectomy causes an abrupt loss of ovarian hormones, including estradiol, progesterone, and testosterone, and several observational studies have associated this change with a higher risk of later cognitive impairment or dementia, particularly when surgery is performed at a younger age. However, these studies have assessed different outcomes, including dementia, mild cognitive impairment, subjective cognitive changes, and AD-related imaging findings, and current evidence does not establish a direct causal relationship between oophorectomy and AD. Possible biological pathways include neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, amyloid-β and tau-related changes, and cerebrovascular dysfunction, although much of the mechanistic evidence remains experimental or indirect. Genetic background, vascular health, age at surgery, and the duration of hormone deprivation may further influence individual risk. Hormone replacement therapy has an established role in the management of premature or early surgical menopause when there is no contraindication, but its effect on long-term AD prevention remains uncertain; the timing of treatment may be important, but current evidence does not confirm a preventive effect. This review summarizes current epidemiological, neuroimaging, and experimental evidence linking oophorectomy with cognitive health and AD, and discusses hormone therapy, pharmacological and non-pharmacological management, emerging research approaches, and remaining knowledge gaps. Future studies with detailed information on surgical timing, hormone exposure, genetic risk, vascular factors, longitudinal cognition, and AD-related biomarkers are needed to better define which women may be most vulnerable after premenopausal oophorectomy.
Authors: Xu S; Fu X; Zuo L; Wang M

Title: miR-214-3p and NCKAP1: A microglial functional dimension of Alzheimer's progression.
Abstract: Biological Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology does not fully explain the marked heterogeneity in clinical severity or progression. We investigated whether patient-derived induced microglia-like cell (iMG) profiles capture a functional dimension of AD progression beyond conventional plasma biomarkers. We studied 114 participants comprising amyloid-negative healthy controls (n = 18) and amyloid-positive AD-continuum groups (cognitively unimpaired, n = 2; mild cognitive impairment, n = 18; AD dementia, n = 76). Plasma biomarkers, patient-derived iMG phagocytic function, and molecular markers were measured from the same blood draw. Longitudinal clinical follow-up was available in 102 participants, and paired baseline/follow-up blood samples were analyzed in a longitudinal biomarker cohort (n = 38). iMG phagocytic capacity progressively declined across the AD continuum, accompanied by reduced NCK-associated protein 1 (NCKAP1) expression and the strongest association with plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Baseline NCKAP1 primarily reflected current cognitive impairment, whereas plasma miR-214-3p independently predicted faster cognitive decline beyond plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p-tau217), GFAP, neurofilament light chain (NfL), age, and baseline cognition. Within amyloid-positive AD dementia, plasma miR-214-3p identified rapidly progressive disease and substantially improved prognostic discrimination beyond conventional plasma biomarkers. Longitudinally, declining NCKAP1 and increasing plasma miR-214-3p tracked the rate of cognitive deterioration, whereas plasma p-tau217, GFAP, and NfL changed over time but did not track disease tempo. Patient-derived iMG profiling identifies microglial phagocytic dysfunction as a complementary functional dimension of AD progression beyond conventional plasma biomarkers. Longitudinal microglial dynamics tracked disease tempo more closely than conventional plasma pathology markers and may help interpret biological-clinical discordance, supporting biologically informed staging, prognosis, and patient stratification in AD.
Authors: Noh MY; Moon Y; Kang S; Moon WJ; Kim HJ; Seo SW; Ahn S; Kang MH; Kim YS; Kim H; Bae JS; Jin HK; Choi H; Koh SH; Park KH; Day GS; Bu G; Kim SH
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: BAG3 coordinates astrocytic proteostasis of Alzheimer's disease-linked proteins via proteasome, autophagy, and retromer interactions.
Abstract: Bcl-2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3) is a mediator of chaperone-assisted selective autophagy, and in the brain, is most highly expressed in astrocytes. However, its role in astrocytes remains poorly defined. Given the genetic and pathological links of BAG3 to proteostasis and neurodegenerative diseases, we investigated how BAG3 contributes to astrocyte function and Alzheimer's disease (AD). To define its function and relevance, we used single-nucleus RNA sequencing to confirm BAG3 enrichment in astrocytes and employed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of human induced pluripotent stem cells followed by proteomic and transcriptomic profiling, which revealed that BAG3 loss caused greater disruption in astrocytes than in neurons. BAG3-deficient astrocytes displayed reduced autophagy, lysosomal abundance and activity, and proteasome function. Coimmunoprecipitation identified BAG3 known binding partners (e.g., HSPB8, proteasome regulators), as well as an interactor in the retromer complex, VPS35. BAG3 deficiency resulted in altered retromer activity as measured by amyloid precursor protein (APP) localization in endosomes. In addition to validating these binding partners, integrative -omics analyses showed that BAG3 regulates AD-relevant proteins (GFAP, BIN1), as well as HSPB8. Functionally, BAG3 knockout astrocytes exhibited impaired amyloid-β proteostasis when cocultured with APP/PSEN1 mutant neurons, directly linking BAG3 to a disease-relevant astrocyte phenotype. Finally, analysis of postmortem human brain revealed that BAG3 expression marks a stress-responsive astrocyte subtype in aged individuals. Together, these findings demonstrate that BAG3 coordinates astrocyte proteostasis through interactions with regulators of autophagy, proteasome activity, and retromer function, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target and central node of astrocytic protein quality control in neurodegeneration.
Authors: Augur ZM; Fogo GM; Benoit CR; Kearney MA; Terzioglu G; Murphy ZR; Arbery MR; Comandante-Lou N; Duong DM; Seyfried NT; De Jager PL; Young-Pearse TL
Journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

Title: Cross-cohort NULISAseq identifies tau-anchored CSF and plasma-specific signatures across the amyloid-positive Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: ATN-stratified cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomic signals may partly reflect classifier tau immunoassays; reproducible non-tau signals and CSF-plasma differences remain unclear. We profiled CSF from 60 A<sup>+</sup> Beijing patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and 875 A<sup>+</sup> Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel. Differential expression was assessed using a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 and |log<sub>2</sub>FC|≥0.5 across three ATN contrasts. We also analyzed ADNI plasma, protein-cognition correlations, tau-adjusted associations, and nested models comparing non-tau proteins with tau biomarkers. Eight CSF proteins met the cross-cohort criterion within at least one matched contrast: pTau-217, pTau-181, pTau-231, MAPT, SMOC1, MDH1, VSNL1, and FABP3. NULISA tau correlated with INNOTEST (ρ = 0.75-0.85) and Elecsys (ρ = 0.65-0.68). T and N classifications agreed for 94.6% of ADNI participants (κ = 0.880); after adjustment for CSF pTau-217, all 12 associations involving the four non-tau proteins retained their direction and FDR support. In CSF, Elecsys p-tau181 and NULISA tau-family analytes had the strongest cognitive correlations (mean |ρ| = 0.35 and 0.29-0.34, respectively), followed by FABP3 (0.24). Adding the four-protein block after tau increased cross-validated R<sup>2</sup> across all three cross-sectional outcomes in models without diagnosis (+0.0101 to +0.0265), most clearly for the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale, 13-item version (ADAS-Cog13); diagnosis-conditioned models showed no stable increment beyond tau and clinical characteristics. In plasma, pTau-217 was the only analyte that met both thresholds in all three contrasts. CSF NULISAseq identified a reproducible tau-associated signature across A<sup>+</sup> cohorts that extended beyond the tau family. The four non-tau proteins extend the molecular profile associated with tau-defined disease state and merit further evaluation for biological stratification in independent cohorts.
Authors: Ding L; Zheng M; Wang S; Liu W; Liang Y; Xie S; Yang T; Sheng D; Wang S; Sheng J; Jia J
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Glutamate, Immune Cells and Alzheimer's Disease: An Attempt to Link the Triad.
Abstract: Glutamate (Glu), although the main excitatory neurotransmitter (NT) of the central nervous system (CNS), evidence recognizes its role in influencing immune cell function and activation, including cytokine production, cell proliferation, migration, and survival. Importantly, dysregulation of Glu homeostasis has been implicated in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD), a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, neuronal loss and neuroinflammation. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biochemistry of the glutamatergic synapse, as well as the expression and signaling of Glu receptors (GluRs) in human immune cells. Furthermore, it examines two major hypotheses of AD pathogenesis -the glutamatergic and the neuroimmune hypothesis- and proposes a unified glutamatergic-neuroimmune framework. In this model, disrupted glutamatergic signaling at the neuron-glia-immune interface may represent a central contributor to AD pathology. Understanding the glutamatergic-neuroimmune axis may provide novel insights into therapeutic strategies targeting neuroimmune modulation in AD.
Authors: Chinas NA; Alexopoulos H

Title: MIND diet-related plasma proteins are associated with Alzheimer's disease risk.
Abstract: Adherence to the Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet is associated with reduced dementia risk, but underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Plasma proteomics (SomaScan 7k) from 206 Indiana Alzheimer's Disease Research Center participants were analyzed using network analysis to identify modules associated with MIND diet scores. Diet-related hub proteins were then investigated for associations with Alzheimer's disease (AD) phenotypes and as potential diet-AD outcome mediators. Validation analyses were conducted in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study (n = 10,228) and Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium (n = 3,723) datasets. Higher MIND diet scores were associated with lower AD odds (odds ratio = 0.75, p = 0.01) and lower plasma neurofilament light chain levels (β = -0.07, p = 0.02). Two proteins, MCTS1 and cytidylate kinase, were associated with MIND diet and AD risk, and may mediate their relationship (p[a × b < 0] ≥ 0.95). Validation analyses supported the MCTS1 finding. Vascular-related biological mechanisms may underlie associations between diet and dementia risk.
Authors: Fernandez S; Dempsey DA; Chaudhuri S; Huang YN; Park T; Liu S; Unverzagt FW; Gao S; Wilcock DM; Yang J; Rebholz CM; Risacher SL; Saykin AJ; Nho K
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Sex-specific brain reserve and progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease dementia.
Abstract: Sex differences exist in Alzheimer's disease (AD) treatment response, but the role of sex in disease development and progression remains unclear. We performed multimodal analyses of AD biomarker-positive individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; MCI n = 593, AD n = 270) and National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (MCI n = 436, AD n = 174). Baseline gray matter volume (GMV) was compared by sex. In ADNI, tau positron emission tomography burden and cerebrospinal fluid growth-associated protein 43 (GAP-43) were assessed. Longitudinal analyses examined atrophy and conversion from MCI to dementia. Females with MCI exhibited greater baseline GMV than males primarily in the thalamus, caudate, cerebellum, postcentral gyrus, and middle cingulate gyrus, with no differences at the AD stage. Despite this, females exhibited higher baseline GAP-43, greater tau burden in temporal and parietal regions, and more rapid annual hippocampal atrophy. Conversion rates were similar. Findings suggest that females may tolerate greater pathology at early stages but experience faster neurodegeneration later, supporting sex-specific disease trajectories and highlighting the need for sex-informed biomarkers.
Authors: Liu X; de Boer SCM; Tartaglia MC
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Mechanisms of Brain Aging and Their Links to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Disease Pathology.
Abstract: Brain aging is a major risk factor for neurodegenerative disorders and is associated with a progressive loss of neuronal homeostasis. Rather than resulting from a single pathological event, brain aging involves coordinated changes across multiple biological processes, including neuroinflammation, proteostasis impairment, mitochondrial dysfunction, neurotransmission deficit, cellular senescence, gut microbiota dysbiosis, extracellular vesicle dysregulation, nutrient-sensing disturbances, and metabolic drift. These processes interact across molecular, cellular, and systemic levels and may progressively increase neuronal vulnerability to neurodegenerative pathology. Age-related biological alterations may increase susceptibility to Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. Disease-associated proteins, including amyloid-β, tau, and α-synuclein, may interact with age-related inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis. This review examines the evidence supporting these mechanisms, their interactions, and their relevance to normal brain aging, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease. Because much of the current mechanistic evidence derives from animal and cellular models, further longitudinal and human studies are needed to provide a more complete understanding of how these mechanisms operate during human brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases.
Authors: Yi H; Qin H; Goon JA; Makpol S; Tan JK

Title: Blood transcriptomic signatures of vascular risk in Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Lifestyle and environmental factors contributing to cardiovascular risk are components of the exposome, yet molecular signatures associated with cumulative cardiovascular risk in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain incompletely understood. We analyzed blood-based transcriptomics data from two independent cohorts: Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH; N = 148, Korean) and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; N = 743, predominantly European ancestry). Framingham cardiovascular risk score (FRS)-associated co-expression network modules were identified, followed by pathway-based enrichment, hub gene-based participant stratification, and bidirectional cross-cohort discovery-replication analyses. Two co-expression modules were associated with FRS in SNUBH, and six in ADNI. Bidirectional analyses identified two preserved modules with consistent module-FRS associations across cohorts, enriched in pathways implicated in cellular responses to exposure, including RNA-protein homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and hematopoietic processes. Hub genes in the two modules stratified participants into molecularly distinct subgroups concordant with clinical FRS categories. FRS-associated molecular pathways were identified and warrant further investigation as potential targets for risk modification.
Authors: Han SW; Park YH; Pyun JM; Hwang J; Park JS; Kim S; Nho K
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Dorsal and ventral stream visuoperceptual processing deficits in Lewy body disease.
Abstract: Hypometabolism of visual-processing cortices is the hallmark of dementia in Lewy body diseases (LBD) yet visuoperceptual impairments remain under-researched compared to other cognitive domains. Novel, sensitive measures of dorsal- and ventral-stream visual processing were developed and administered to n=53 LBD patients, spanning cognitively asymptomatic to dementia, and compared to n=29 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. Further analyses stratified LBD for visual hallucination status and contrasted visuoperceptual performance to measures of attention/executive function. Visuoperceptual impairments were more prominent in LBD than AD, being detectable even in some that were cognitively asymptomatic. LBD demonstrated comparable ventral and dorsal impairments, whereas ventral visuoperceptual performance was relatively preserved compared to dorsal in AD. In LBD, visuoperceptual impairments were strongly associated with visual hallucination and explained a significant amount of performance on visually presented executive function/attention measures. The effect sizes of impairment in demented LBD were substantially larger on the novel visuoperceptual tests compared to standard non-visually presented tests of attention (Digit Span) and executive function (phonemic fluency). Early dorsal and ventral stream impairments are a hallmark of dementia in LBD, differing quantitatively and qualitatively from AD. These deficits in LBD were more pronounced than those of attention and executive function.
Authors: McCann E; Coleman F; Lee S; Fazlollahi A; O'Sullivan JD; Nestor PJ

Title: Real-World Patient Eligibility for Alzheimer's Disease Anti-Amyloid Therapy in Seven Swedish Memory Clinics.
Abstract: Anti-amyloid therapies lecanemab and donanemab are the first potentially disease-modifying treatments for Alzheimer's disease (AD) approved in Europe. We estimated real-world eligibility for these treatments in a large multicenter memory clinic patient cohort in Sweden (MemClin). MemClin included patients with a first diagnostic visit between 2016 and 2022 at seven specialist memory clinics in Stockholm, Sweden. To estimate eligibility for anti-amyloid therapy, we applied key inclusion/exclusion criteria from the lecanemab and donanemab appropriate use recommendations. Eligible patients were required to have (1) a clinical diagnosis of AD-type dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI), (2) confirmed Aβ pathology (abnormal CSF Aβ42) and (3) no apparent medical exclusion criteria. Eligibility was calculated for different scenarios to provide both upper-bound estimates (main analysis) and more conservative, implementation-ready estimates of near-term treatable patients (sensitivity analysis). Cohort consisted of 2126 patients (mean age 77.1 ± 6.6 years; 61.8% MCI, 24.2% dementia, 13.7% subjective cognitive impairment). In the main analysis, 11.5% of the whole cohort was estimated to be eligible for either treatment (lecanemab 10.6%, donanemab 11.5%). Most eligible patients had early-stage disease (61.9% MCI vs. 38.1% dementia) and an A + T- biomarker profile, that is, normal biomarker of tau (57.9%). Eligibility was markedly lower in sensitivity analyses (e.g., 2.7% when all patients without MRI were assumed ineligible). Even upper-bound estimates indicate that a minority of real-world memory clinic patients may currently qualify for anti-amyloid therapy. These findings provide timely evidence to inform the ongoing debate on the implementation of anti-amyloid therapy in public healthcare.
Authors: Rosenberg A; Rennie A; Ekman U; Daniilidou M; Hall A; Matton A; Solomon A; Wahlund LO; Kivipelto M; Westman E

Title: Preclinical and first-in-human evaluation of VG-3927/SAR448851, an oral small-molecule TREM2 agonist for Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Microglial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, with loss-of-function variants in the microglial receptor TREM2 as major risk factors for late-onset AD. We report VG-3927, an oral, CNS-penetrant small-molecule TREM2 agonist that engages the transmembrane domains of TREM2 and its adaptor DAP12 to promote higher-order receptor complex formation and downstream signaling. VG-3927 and tool compound VG-3909 exhibited (sub)nanomolar potency, cooperated with endogenous ligands including amyloid-β (Aβ), and restored signaling in disease-associated TREM2 variants. In human iPSC-derived neuron-microglia-astrocyte cultures, VG-3927 reduced inflammatory cytokines and markers of neuronal damage. In 5xFAD amyloidosis mice expressing the common variant of hTREM2 (5xFAD;hTREM2CV), VG-3909 induced neuroprotective transcriptional reprogramming of microglia, particularly in the plaque niche; enhanced Aβ phagocytosis; and boosted brain glucose metabolism. By contrast, a TREM2 agonist antibody, which may be sequestered by soluble TREM2 (sTREM2), failed to engage plaque microglia. In a first-in-human, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial (NCT06343636, n = 115), VG-3927 was well tolerated across single and multiple ascending doses of up to 140 milligrams. Pharmacokinetics supported once-daily dosing with high CNS penetration (CSF-to-unbound plasma ratio of 0.91). VG-3927 induced dose-dependent reductions in CSF sTREM2, a biomarker of target engagement, consistent across healthy and elderly participants and participants with AD, supporting further clinical development in AD under the new designation SAR448851.
Authors: Dejanovic B; Figley MD; Weisman E; Kiragasi B; Gergits FW; Larson K; Renoux A; Rajagovindan R; Pandya B; Houze J; Huang L; Gaudreault F; O'Mara R; Clarkson JH; Turnbull MT; Meier A; Colonna M; Stromme J; Gray D; Thackaberry EA; Kaufmann P; Mirescu C

Title: Ionizing radiation and Alzheimer's disease: epidemiology, mechanisms, and eCIRP-mediated tau pathology.
Abstract: As human radiation exposure expands through medical imaging, nuclear industry growth, and the acceleration of crewed space exploration, understanding the molecular mechanisms linking radiation to Alzheimer's disease (AD) is becoming an increasingly urgent priority. Here, we review epidemiological, mechanistic, and therapeutic evidence for a relationship between ionizing radiation and AD, focusing on a neuroinflammatory pathway centered on extracellular cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (eCIRP). Epidemiological support comes from occupational cohorts of nuclear workers and studies linking residential radon to AD mortality; a meta-analysis of 18 studies finds an 11% increased all-cause dementia risk per 100 mSv. Mechanistically, ionizing radiation generates DNA double-strand breaks and reactive oxygen species that activate the ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase and trigger rapid microglial activation, and causes the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic translocation and extracellular release of the danger-associated molecular pattern eCIRP. Released eCIRP activates neuronal cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5), resulting in AD-like tau phosphorylation. This pathway is validated by loss-of-function studies in CIRP-knockout mice and pharmacological blockade with the eCIRP inhibitor C23. Beyond tau phosphorylation, eCIRP drives mitochondrial dysfunction and ferroptosis in myeloid cells and activates endothelial cell death pathways that may compromise blood-brain barrier integrity. eCIRP links radiation-induced neuroinflammation to tau-driven neurodegeneration, and eCIRP inhibitors warrant investigation for both radiation-induced cognitive dysfunction and sporadic AD, where eCIRP is similarly elevated. Translating these mechanistic insights into eCIRP-targeted therapies and validated biomarkers could open a new front in the prevention and treatment of these prevalent and debilitating disorders.
Authors: Brenner M; Sharma A; Wang P

Title: Simultaneous Visualization of Labile Ferrous Iron Pool and Biothiols Reveals Divergent Pathological Trajectories in Ferroptosis and Alzheimer's Disease.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and ferroptosis share certain pathobiochemical features, yet the spatiotemporal evolution patterns and metabolic trajectories of their core hallmarks, labile ferrous iron pool and biothiols, and their pathophysiological relationship remain elusive. Herein, we developed a single-molecule dual-site fluorescent probe, FCG, for simultaneous discrimination of Fe2+, Cys/Hcy, and GSH via analyte-specific cascade reaction mechanisms. The probe exhibits rapid kinetics (k = 0.16-1.23 min-1), nanomolar sensitivity (detection limits: 38.8-509.2 nM), and well-separated emission signatures (Δλem ≥ 60 nm), facilitating concurrent visualization of these endogenous species dynamics in living systems. Importantly, application to cellular and mouse models revealed divergent metabolic pathways: ferroptosis displays synchronized labile ferrous iron pool accumulation, catastrophic lipid peroxidation, and global biothiols depletion, whereas AD exhibits modest iron elevation, a unique biothiols profile (elevated total Cys and Hcy but depleted GSH), and protein aggregation that is absent in ferroptosis. Comparative proteomic analysis further elucidated the molecular landscape of these dynamically regulated networks, as well as their distinct pathological metabolic trajectories. This study not only clarifies the mechanistic basis for the fundamentally different pathological trajectories underlying ferroptosis and AD but also provides critical evidence and analytical tools for targeted interventions in neurodegenerative diseases.
Authors: Yin G; Tan W; Wang D; He Z; Dou C; Wang H; Lu Q; Zhong G; Du F; Yin P

Title: Cortical thickness signature of early-onset Alzheimer's disease across clinical stages and A/T1 biomarker profiles.
Abstract: The cortical thinning signature of early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD) is well established in dementia, but its emergence during earlier disease stages remains unclear. We investigated when it becomes detectable and whether it differs according to fluid amyloid and phosphorylated-tau (A/T1) biomarker profiles. We studied 292 individuals <65 years who underwent 3T structural MRI and cerebrospinal fluid assessment of Aβ42/40 and p-tau181. Participants were classified as A-T1- subjective cognitive decline (SCD; reference group), A+T1-, or A+T1+. Cortical thickness and hippocampal volume were measured using FreeSurfer. EOAD signature regions were defined by comparing biomarker-confirmed AD dementia with the reference group and subsequently examined across A/T1 profiles in SCD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Brain-cognition associations were assessed. The cohort comprised 107 reference and 185 amyloid-positive participants (76 A+T1- and 109 A+T1+). EOAD dementia was characterized by marked cortical thinning in posterior parietal and lateral temporal regions. In MCI, cortical thinning was focal in A+T1-, but more extensive in A+T1+ who also showed hippocampal atrophy. At the SCD stage, focal thinning of the EOAD signature, precuneus, and banks of the superior temporal sulcus was observed in A+T1+, whereas no structural alterations were detected in A+T1-. Cortical thinning was associated with episodic and visuospatial memory performance in MCI, while no brain-cognition associations were observed in SCD. EOAD-related cortical thinning is detectable before dementia and varies across A/T1 profiles, with combined amyloid and p-tau181 positivity associated with earlier and more extensive structural involvement.
Authors: Zilioli A; Mohanty R; Rosenberg A; Matton A; Granberg T; Hagman G; Spallazzi M; Kivipelto M; Westman E

Title: Novel NIR DDNP-type solvatochromic and fluorogenic probes for amyloid β detection.
Abstract: Selective near-infrared fluorescent probes for amyloid β aggregates are of considerable interest as molecular imaging tools for the diagnosis and study of Alzheimer's disease. Herein, we describe the rational design and synthesis of DDNP-type donor-π-acceptor fluorophores incorporating a fixed N,N-dimethylamino donor group, while systematically modifying seven aromatic π-bridges and four electron-withdrawing acceptor groups to investigate structure-property relationships. The library of 26 probes is a result of multi-step synthetic routes and exhibits pronounced solvatochromic behaviour together with strong fluorogenic responses. Compounds' photophysical properties, including absorption and emission maxima, Stokes shifts, and quantum yields, are systematically evaluated in five solvents of varying polarity. The study reveals clear structure-property relationships, demonstrating the influence of π-bridge length and electron-acceptor strength on the optical characteristics, including near-infrared emission. Selected fluorophores are further assessed for their affinity towards amyloid β fibrils through a combination of in vitro experiments and in silico molecular docking studies. Among the compounds investigated, the N,N-dimethylamino-stilbene-malononitrile derivative emerges as the lead candidate, showing an optimal balance of favourable photophysical properties and strong amyloid β binding affinity. Subsequent evaluation using brain tissue obtained post mortem from a patient with Alzheimer's disease demonstrates selective staining of amyloid β plaques with minimal background fluorescence.
Authors: Rogan M; Blinc L; Rejc L; Martek BA; Vezonik U; Babnik I; Mukaetov B; Rajković AB; Meden A; Pfabe J; Rupnik MS; Jaklin M; Bresjanac M; Gobec S; Knez D; Kladnik J; Košmrlj J

Title: Lactate-Informed Exercise Prescription in Mild Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer's Disease: A Translational Framework for Preserving Cognition, Mobility, and Independence.
Abstract: This narrative review proposes a conceptual, lactate-informed framework for individualized exercise prescription in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD). Exercise is recommended in these populations, but fixed external doses do not account for heterogeneity in disease stage, frailty, sarcopenia, cardiovascular risk, or recovery.
