We integrate clinical exercise evidence, geriatric assessment, lactate physiology, muscle-brain signaling, implementation science, and trial methodology. The framework uses peripheral blood lactate as one component of a monitoring matrix with workload, heart rate, blood pressure, perceived exertion, fatigue recovery, gait safety, adherence, and caregiver support. Repeated, standardized lactate responses are classified as low, adaptive and recoverable, excessive, or non-interpretable/unsafe, prompting stepwise adjustment of aerobic, resistance, balance, and cognitive-motor training. Peripheral blood lactate is an internal-load marker; it does not directly quantify blood-brain barrier transport, CNS lactate kinetics, or target engagement. Mechanistic pathways involving monocarboxylate transport, HCAR1, BDNF/VEGF, myokines, and lactylation therefore remain hypotheses to be tested in humans with MCI or AD. The novelty of the framework is its integration of disease stage, geriatric phenotype, peripheral metabolic response, and recovery into clinically actionable dose decisions rather than a universal lactate threshold. Prospective multicenter trials should standardize sampling, validate response thresholds, and determine whether this approach improves cognition, mobility, independence, safety, and caregiver-relevant outcomes beyond usual advice or fixed-dose exercise.
Authors: Li X

Title: Dysregulated metal homeostasis in Alzheimer's disease: From pathological modulators to therapeutic targets.
Abstract: The "metal ion hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained widespread acceptance, but translating this understanding into effective therapies remains elusive. This likely stems from a simplistic understanding of metal homeostasis as merely a matter of "excess and deficiency." This article reviews the context-dependent roles of iron, copper, zinc, aluminum, and manganese in the pathogenesis of AD, with a particular focus on their bidirectional interactions with classic AD pathology (the ferroptosis hypothesis is relatively mature, while emerging hypotheses such as cuproptosis have not been fully elucidated). Metal homeostasis dysregulation can directly promote β-amyloid aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Conversely, these pathological processes can also alter the binding, storage, transport, and subcellular distribution of metal ions. Dysregulated metal ions function as "context-dependent" modulators of pathological processes. Their functional effects depend on metal species, concentration, binding state, subcellular compartment, and disease stage. Metal homeostasis dysregulation associated with AD may essentially reflect a redistribution between physiological and pathological pools. Ideal interventions should selectively neutralize pathological metal pools while preserving or restoring essential metal-dependent neuronal functions. By integrating the latest advances in the field of metal-targeted therapies (chelators, metabolic modulators, biomarkers, metal imaging, and gene editing), we emphasize that future treatments should shift from nonspecific metal clearance toward precise metal regulation and precision medicine.
Authors: Yang J; Lou F; Sun W; Li M; Su L; Wang Y; Li P; Su J

Title: Effects of hyperbaric oxygen therapy in the treatment of selected diseases of the nervous system.
Abstract: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) has attracted increasing interest as a potential supportive intervention in neurological disorders. By increasing the amount of oxygen dissolved in blood plasma, HBOT enhances oxygen delivery to hypoxic tissues and may influence mechanisms involved in neuroplasticity, inflammation, and tissue repair. Experimental and clinical studies suggest that HBOT may support neurological recovery in selected conditions, particularly following ischemic or traumatic brain injury. However, the effectiveness of HBOT varies depending on the underlying disease, and further high-quality clinical studies are needed to establish its role in neurological rehabilitation.The article was based on an analysis of data from Google Scholar and PubMed regarding the effects of hyperbaric therapy.
Authors: Izhytska NV; Sobczyk KA; Ogrodnik KW; Mazurkiewicz M; Malentowicz D; Szafraniec NJ

Title: Mitochondrial carbonic anhydrase-VB inhibition rescues brain endothelial stress and memory in Alzheimer's disease models.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder with no effective cure, characterized by the cerebral parenchymal and vascular accumulation of aggregated amyloid-β (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylated tau. Cerebrovascular and mitochondria dysfunction are early causal events in the progression of AD. Previous studies support that inhibiting carbonic anhydrases (CAs) may prevent mitochondrial and cerebrovascular dysfunction in AD models. Here, we selectively target the mitochondrial CA isoform CA-VB by pharmacological and genetic manipulation in human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells (hCMEC), and we confirm the protective effects of the CA-V inhibitor in AD mice. CA-V inhibition and CA-VB KO prevent Aβ induced mitochondria-mediated endothelial apoptosis, loss of barrier resistance, and hCMEC inflammatory activation. Strikingly, CA-V inhibition also mitigates caspase activation and endothelial cell activation in the brains of 3xTg AD mice, resulting in preserved memory function. Our results demonstrate that selective CA-V inhibition is an effective and promising strategy against AD-mediated cerebrovascular pathology, neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment.
Authors: Lemon NL; Canepa E; Vázquez-Torres R; Parodi-Rullán R; Hirt T; Petersohn LM; Rifat T; Abyaneh MH; Ilies MA; Fossati S

Title: Chronic Conditions in Residential Care Communities: United States, 2025.
Abstract: This report uses 2025 National Post-acute and Long-term Care Study (NPALS) data to examine the characteristics of residential care communities that reported four selected chronic conditions among their current residents: Alzheimer disease and other dementias, heart disease, diabetes, and depression. Data are presented overall and by selected organizational characteristics and adverse events. Data for this report are from the residential care community survey component of the 2025 wave of the biennial NPALS, conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics. Data analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4, SAS-callable SUDAAN version 11.0.3, and Stata/SE version 17. Analyses accounted for the study's complex survey design, included complex survey weights, and used appropriate subsetting techniques. All estimates presented meet the NCHS standards for confidentiality and reliability unless indicated otherwise. In 2025, almost one-half of residential care communities reported all four selected chronic conditions (48%)-Alzheimer disease or other dementias, diabetes, depression, and heart disease-diagnosed among their current residents. Larger (11 or more beds), nonmetropolitan, Northeast, and Midwest residential care communities more commonly reported having all four conditions represented. A higher percentage of nonprofit (54.3%) and chain-affiliated (54.3%) residential care communities, as well as communities using electronic health records (56.7%), reported having all four chronic conditions represented. Residential care communities that reported adverse events among their residents (emergency department visits, hospitalizations, or falls) showed a higher prevalence of having all four conditions represented.
Authors: Caffrey C; Sengupta M; Lendon JP; Kindilien S; Melekin A

Title: Purine metabolism disruption links pathology and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Purine metabolism dysregulation has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its temporal dynamics and mechanistic links to core pathologies remain unclear. This translational study integrated a longitudinal preclinical AD mouse model and clinical cohort investigations to define the role of purine metabolism in AD progression. In APPswe/PSEN1dE9 (APP/PS1) mice, serum-untargeted metabolomics identified purine metabolism as the most notably altered pathway, with metabolite levels (e.g., adenine, adenosine) shifting dynamically across disease stages alongside increasing amyloid-β (Aβ) burden. In the pathology-defined clinical cohort, targeted analysis revealed that serum uric acid and allantoin were specifically depleted in the Aβ+ cognitively impaired (CI) group and correlated strongly with higher brain Aβ load, increased neuroinflammation, and poorer cognitive scores. Formal mediation analysis elucidated a plausible mechanistic cascade: the association of uric acid/allantoin with cognitive impairment was primarily mediated by Aβ pathology. Two-year longitudinal data further suggest that changes in specific purine metabolites might predict the rate of cognitive decline. Allantoin supplementation reduced Aβ pathology through promoting microglial phagocytosis of Aβ in APP/PS1 mice. Our findings identified purine metabolism as a key hub connecting Aβ pathology, neuroinflammation, and clinical progression in AD.
Authors: Qian X; Wang Z; Chen S; Xue Y; Yang Y; Cui P; Zhang M; Tang H

Title: Towards Improved P2X7R Cellular Models for Alzheimer's Disease Drug Discovery.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no disease-modifying therapeutics. The P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) presents as a promising target for AD drug discovery due to its pathogenic role in the onset and progression of neuroinflammation, a hallmark pathology of AD. There has been extensive pre-clinical work on the development of P2X7R antagonists, but there is yet to be a therapeutic that has progressed for further clinical evaluation in Alzheimer's disease. To accelerate the discovery and translation of P2X7R antagonists for AD, better in vitro screening models are needed. Current models such as immortalized cell lines fail to replicate the complexity of physiological disease, and animal models present hurdles due to poor translatability, and low accuracy in predicting safety and efficacy of therapeutics. However, induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) may allow bridging of the gap between preclinical screening methods and human disease. These patient-derived cells allow the genetic material of donors to be harvested, better recapitulating the multifaceted aspects of disease. iPSC-derived neurons and glia may facilitate the creation of more successful disease modelling and drug screening platforms, allowing for a greater understanding of the underlying disease pathology. Current work in the central nervous system (CNS) drug discovery space has demonstrated that the P2X7R is functional in disease-relevant iPSC models, supporting their suitability for pharmacological investigation. More importantly, they provide a robust platform that may drive the development of P2X7R antagonists from pre-clinical studies into a clinical setting.
Authors: Agius CTA; McKenzie ADJ; Woollett K; Werry EL; Kassiou M

Title: Therapeutic Administration of Malva parviflora Hydroalcoholic Extract Restores Cognitive Function Consistent with a Resilient Phenotype in Female 5XFAD.
Abstract: The remarkable increase in human life expectancy has been accompanied by a rising global incidence of neurodegenerative disorders, particularly Alzheimer's disease. This condition is characterized by progressive accumulation of soluble and insoluble amyloid-beta peptides, neuroinflammation, and synaptic dysfunction in the hippocampus, leading to impaired higher-order cognition. Epidemiological evidence indicates that women are disproportionately affected; however, female-specific pathology remains understudied. Here, we evaluated the therapeutic potential of a hydroalcoholic extract of Malva parviflora in female 5XFAD mice following prolonged intragastric administration initiated after disease establishment. Long-term treatment shifted cognitive performance toward a phenotype comparable to wild-type littermates, an improvement associated with reduced soluble amyloid-beta levels in the hippocampus and peripheral circulation, and significant attenuation of reactive astrogliosis as evidenced by reduced hippocampal glial fibrillary acidic protein levels. Because reactive astrocytes impair synaptic activity and metabolic homeostasis during disease progression, we examined the direct effects of Malva parviflora on synaptic plasticity ex vivo. Incubation of hippocampal synaptosomes from adult female 5XFAD mice with the extract restored chemically induced long-term potentiation. These findings demonstrate that Malva parviflora attenuates key pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease and promotes cognitive recovery, supporting its potential as a plant-derived therapeutic candidate, particularly in females most affected by Alzheimer's disease. Future studies including both sexes under a therapeutic paradigm are needed to determine the generalizability of these findings.
Authors: Rojas-Sánchez I; Cortes-Flores E; Camacho-Concha N; Almazán JL; Ramírez-Lugo L; Crivelli-Galindo E; Ramirez-Serrano CE; Pedraza-Alva G; Pérez-Martínez L

Title: Neurological and systemic adverse event reporting patterns for lecanemab: A global WHO VigiAccess analysis.
Abstract: Lecanemab is an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody approved for early Alzheimer disease. Evaluation of spontaneous reports may complement clinical-trial evidence by identifying real-world adverse-event reporting patterns. This study aimed to characterize lecanemab-associated adverse drug reaction reports in the World Health Organization VigiAccess database at the System Organ Class (SOC) and Preferred term (PT) levels. A retrospective descriptive pharmacovigilance analysis was conducted using VigiAccess data from database inception through 13 September 2026. Frequencies and percentages were calculated for SOCs, PTs, demographic characteristics, geographic regions, and reporting years. Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated for principal reporting proportions. VigiAccess contained 3212 individual safety reports comprising 5358 adverse drug reaction events. Nervous system disorders constituted the largest SOC (n = 1827; 34.10%; 95% confidence interval: 32.84-35.38), followed by general disorders and administration-site conditions (n = 1015; 18.94%; 95% confidence interval: 17.92-20.01). The most frequently reported PTs were headache (n = 512; 9.56%), amyloid-related imaging abnormality-edema/effusion (n = 360; 6.72%), amyloid-related imaging abnormality-microhemorrhages and hemosiderin deposits (n = 326; 6.08%), chills (n = 281; 5.24%), pyrexia (n = 272; 5.08%), and infusion-related reaction (n = 235; 4.39%). Females accounted for 52.21% of reports, patients aged ≥ 65 years for 62.95%, and the Americas for 80.23%. Most reports (95.73%) were recorded during 2024 to 2026. Neurological, amyloid-related imaging abnormality, systemic, and infusion-associated events were prominent in spontaneous reporting for lecanemab. These findings describe reporting patterns and should not be interpreted as incidence rates or causal associations. Continued patient-level and exposure-adjusted surveillance is required to further characterize lecanemab safety.
Authors: Alorfi NM; Algarni AS

Title: Erebosis: An Emerging Concept of a New Type of Regulated Cell Death.
Abstract: This review briefly describes the discovery of a morphologically distinct form of regulated cell death in Drosophila, termed erebosis, which is characterized by organelle loss, nuclear flattening, and intracellular accumulation of Ance. The latter serves as a biomarker of this type of cell death but does not act as its trigger. Erebosis can be induced by amino acid deprivation accompanied by the reduced cytoplasmic viscosity, and its development is also associated with the increased heme oxygenase activity and decreased intracellular heme levels. We hypothesize that the heme-sensing protein E75 in Drosophila melanogaster, a homolog of mammalian REV-ERB proteins involved in circadian regulation, may provide a link between erebosis and renewal of enterocytes from the intestinal stem cells. Finally, we discuss the differences between erebosis and other forms of regulated cell death, as well as detection of ACE2 in the brains of mice in different models of Alzheimer's disease.
Authors: Nikulin SV; Hushpulian DM; Zakharyants AA; Thomas B; Kazakov SV; Gazaryan IG

Title: Probiotics attenuate AlCl₃-induced Alzheimer's disease via gut-brain axis modulation and suppression of NF-κB/NLRP3 neuroinflammation.
Abstract: Disruptions along the brain-gut-microbiota axis significantly contribute to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of a multi-strain probiotic mixture in mitigating cognitive decline, neuroinflammation, and amyloid pathology in an AD rat model. In the present study, after induction of AD in rats by oral administration of AlCl<sub>3</sub> (50 mg/kg) for 28 days, followed by oral treatment with a probiotic mixture (10<sup>9</sup> log CFU/ml) for 42 days. Behavioral assessments were conducted during the final week. Hippocampal tissues were obtained for histopathological and gene expression analyses and fecal samples were subjected to full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing via Oxford Nanopore approach. Probiotics significantly improved AD-induced deficits in locomotor activity, exploratory behavior, and spatial recognition memory. Histological analysis revealed marked reductions in hippocampal β-amyloid deposition and substantial restoration of colonic mucosal barrier integrity. Microbiota profiling showed that probiotics reversed dysbiosis, significantly enriching beneficial genera (Blautia, Clostridium, Eubacterium). Blautia abundance was strongly negatively correlated with NF-κB expression. Mechanistically, probiotics suppressed neuroinflammation by down-regulating pro-inflammatory cascades TNF-α, NLRP3, IL-1β, and NF-κB activation. Furthermore, treatment suppressed amyloidogenic processing via decreased APP mRNA and enhanced Aβ clearance through upregulation of LRP1 and modulation of AGER. These findings provide integrative evidence that probiotics exert neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects, supporting their translational potential as a preventive strategy against AD-related cognitive decline.
Authors: Elfiky AM; Shahy EM; Mahmoud AA

Title: Menopause and Alzheimer's disease: can hormone replacement therapy modify the risk? A narrative review.
Abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) prevalence and lifetime risk are higher in women than men. This led to the hypothesis that menopause, with its associated changes in female hormone homoeostasis, may be an AD risk factor modifiable by hormone replacement therapy (HRT). However, HRT is not without its risks to women's health, and any recommendations must rest on sound evidence. Here, we critically review data concerning sex-specific epidemiological and biological parameters that may influence AD development. Recent epidemiological studies suggest that the age-adjusted incidence of AD is not higher in women than men. Whilst there is mechanistic experimental evidence that female sex hormones modulate the metabolism of β-amyloid and tau, the neuropathological hallmarks of AD, no clear conclusions can be drawn from studies conducted in humans. Exposure to HRT may modify the development of AD; however, data are weak and the influence of timing, duration, type of HRT, and ethnic, socioeconomic, educational and genomic factors such as APOE genotype, requires further clarification. Large prospective biobank studies in diverse populations, with long follow-up periods and application of biological consensus criteria for the diagnosis of AD provide opportunities to conclusively clarify the relationship between menopause, HRT therapy and risk for the development of AD. Based on current evidence, HRT cannot be recommended as a generic intervention for the reduction of AD risk in women. Any decision to take HRT must consider the individual circumstances and overall health of a woman.
Authors: Wang JY; Ansorge O

Title: Bioactive Compounds as Putative Molecules of Neuroplasticity: An Epigenetic Perspective.
Abstract: Aging populations face rising Alzheimer's disease (AD) incidence, with emerging links between epigenetic dysregulation and cognitive decline. Given their dynamic nature, epigenetic modifications offer potential targets for nutritional intervention, although current evidence remains largely correlational. This review presents a food science-oriented framework examining how dietary bioactive compounds may associate with neuroplasticity modulation through putative epigenetic pathways, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and noncoding RNAs. While certain food-derived ingredients have shown correlations with epigenetic regulation and gene expression related to synaptic plasticity, direct causal evidence in humans is lacking. We identify key epigenetic regulatory hubs as ingredient-responsive candidate targets, providing new criteria for efficacy assessment and functional food design. These associative insights generate testable hypotheses for developing epigenetic-based nutritional strategies aimed at preventing or delaying age-related cognitive decline, while critically highlighting the gap between correlational findings and causal demonstration.
Authors: Zhao F; Bordoni L; Mao Y; Cao J; Gong F; Hou W; Tao L; Gabbianelli R; Li K
Journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry

Title: Should ApoE4 gene editing therapy be approached with caution when AD is accompanied by retinal neurodegenerative diseases?
Abstract: Apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), and ApoE4-directed gene editing and gene therapy have emerged as promising therapeutic strategies for AD, although they remain investigational and are not yet an established mainstream treatment. Interestingly, however, ApoE4 is reported to be associated with a reduced risk of retinal degenerative diseases such as glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and diabetic retinopathy (DR). Therefore, should ApoE4 gene editing therapy be approached with caution when AD occurs concurrently with glaucoma, AMD, or DR? In view of these and based on the existing literature, the present study detailed the distinct roles of ApoE4 in AD, glaucoma, AMD, and DR, with a purpose to offer valuable insights into subsequent ApoE4 gene editing therapies. We also summarise the ApoE-targeted therapeutic programmes currently in preclinical and early clinical development, delineate the remaining translational challenges, and discuss how patients with coexisting retinal neurodegenerative disease might be evaluated and monitored.
Authors: Wenhua Y; Wenjing M; Yan D; Fei L; Juan C; Xia T; Yu G; Xin L; Yanlin H; Ya G; Xuelin Y; Jing L; Meimin J; Wenyi L; Yilin K; Hongke L; Yating L

Title: A pKa-Guided BBB-Permeable NIR Fluorescent Probe for Tracking Lipid Droplets in Microglia with Neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's Disease.
Abstract: Abnormal accumulation of lipid droplets (LDs), accompanied by altered microenvironmental polarity within the microglia, is closely associated with neuroinflammation and also has been increasingly recognized as an early and dynamic indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Herein, a LD-targeting polarity-sensitive blood-brain barrier (BBB)-permeable near-infrared (NIR) probe, BTDN, was screened by tuning the electron-donating substituents to modulate the pKa values of benzothiadiazole-based derivatives. Endowed with the donor-acceptor-donor (D1-A-D2) architecture and strong intramolecular charge-transfer (ICT) characteristics, the BTDN probe exhibited high sensitivity to polarity change. The BTDN probe displayed suitable physicochemical properties such as a pKa of 7.47 and lipophilicity with a log P of 3.72 for favorable BBB-penetrating efficiency with a permeability percentage of 24.23%. In addition, the BTDN probe showed advantages for fluorescence imaging including NIR emission from 643 to 770 nm with the increased polarity, Stokes shift larger than 308 nm, comparable two-photon absorption capacity with an absorption cross-section of 10 GM at 870 nm, good biocompatibility, and robust photostability. Using this multifunctional BTDN probe, the dynamic fluorescence imaging of accumulation behaviors of LDs in BV2 microglia with neuroinflammation was performed, demonstrating that LD formation may serve as a potential biomarker for neuroinflammation. Furthermore, overproduced LDs within microglia were directly observed in vivo and in tissue sections from the brains of AD mice. This work not only provides an imaging tool for dynamically characterizing LD accumulation in microglia but also provides insights into the relationship between LD accumulation in microglia and AD pathogenesis.
Authors: Zhang Z; Ning Y; Wu Z; Sun J; Gao F

Title: Utility of extracellular vesicles in the diagnosis of central nervous system diseases.
Abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) disorders encompass a diverse spectrum of conditions characterized by intricate pathological mechanisms, and the presence of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) has long impeded early diagnosis. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are lipid bilayer nanoparticles released by living cells that can encapsulate and transport bioactive molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids across the BBB. EVs can be detected in biofluids such as blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) through non-invasive or minimally invasive assays, and have emerged as highly promising vehicles for CNS liquid biopsies. Recent studies demonstrate that specific EV-associated protein cargoes (e.g., phosphorylated tau, α-syn) and non-coding RNAs (e.g., miR-422a, miR-409-3p) exhibit distinct differential expression profiles across various pathologies. These molecular signatures hold promise for early detection, differential diagnosis, and disease staging, with some biomarker panels showing high diagnostic accuracy. However, whether they outperform conventional CSF biomarkers still requires direct comparison and validation within the same cohorts. This review highlights recent research advances in the use of EVs for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, briefly touches upon other CNS disorders including stroke, glioma, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and discusses the clinical translational potential and remaining challenges of EV-based diagnostics.
Authors: Wang M; Yang J; Gao C; Qu S; Mi H; Guo Y; Gui T; Gai Z

Title: Clusterin is enriched in plaque-associated astrocytes and localizes to synapses in Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: The clusterin gene (CLU) is a top genome-wide association studies (GWAS) risk locus for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and elevated clusterin levels have been reported in AD biofluids and brain tissue. Despite growing interest in clusterin as a biomarker and therapeutic target, its cellular and subcellular localization in the human brain remains incompletely understood, in part due to a lack of well-characterized reagents. We generated and validated monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) that distinguish secreted and intracellular clusterin, and applied these tools to human biofluids, brain tissue, and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) -derived astrocytes. The mAbs enabled sensitive detection and quantification of clusterin in plasma, serum, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain tissue homogenates. Immunostaining demonstrated that clusterin is associated with amyloid plaques in AD brain and localizes to synapses in both healthy and AD tissue; the mAb detecting intracellular clusterin demonstrated specific expression in astrocytes, confirmed using astrocytoma lines and iPSC-derived astrocytes. Quantitative analysis demonstrated increased clusterin signal in plaque-associated astrocytes, particularly those surrounding larger plaques. The findings provide better understanding of clusterin expression in the healthy and AD brain, informing roles of clusterin in brain homeostasis and AD pathogenesis.
Authors: Byrne RAJ; Veteleanu A; Cramp HL; Bacon OG; Baillie KL; Bright M; Cooke RS; Fenn GD; Flores Castelán M; Lee KY; Zelek WM; Morgan BP; Daskoulidou N
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Technology-natives and technology-adopters: Age differences in remote cognitive assessment in Alzheimer disease.
Abstract: Cognitive changes in the asymptomatic stages of Alzheimer disease (AD) are subtle and difficult to detect using conventional cognitive tests. High-frequency smartphone-based testing may improve sensitivity to these changes, but generational differences in technology use could influence performance. We examined generational differences in cognition using remote, high-frequency smartphone assessments. Older adults (N = 444) from the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center and young and middle-aged adults (N = 113) from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN) completed an in-clinic cognitive battery and brief smartphone tests up to four times daily for 7 days. We compared adherence, reliability, practice effects, and correlations with in-clinic measures. Older adults showed higher adherence than younger participants (78% vs 59%). Younger adults achieved higher reliability with fewer sessions and exhibited much smaller practice effects. Smartphone to in-clinic test correlations were strong in both young-to-middle-aged and older adults. Generational differences have important implications for the design and implementation of smartphone-based cognitive studies.
Authors: Katteri S; Wilks H; Welhaf M; Aschenbrenner AJ; Frank CC; Vila-Castelar C; Stout S; Sliwinski MJ; Benzinger TL; Florencia Clarens M; Cruchaga C; Daniels A; Day GS; Devenney E; Gordon BA; Huey ED; Ikeuchi T; Ishiguro T; Ibanez L; Jucker M; Karch C; Levin J; Perrin R; Renton A; Supnet-Bell C; Weston PSJ; Xiong C; Libre-Guerra J; McDade EM; Bateman RJ; Morris JC; Hassenstab J
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Marginal Analysis of Clustered Interval-Censored Competing Risks Data With Informative Cluster Size.
Abstract: Motivated by the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) study, this paper addresses the marginal analysis of clustered data under a complex setting involving interval censoring, competing risks, and informative cluster size, for which existing methods are not readily applicable. We consider a class of marginal generalized odds-rate transformation models for the cumulative incidence function in the presence of interval-censored competing risks, with the Fine-Gray model and the sub-distribution proportional odds model included as special cases. For statistical inference, a cluster-weighted sieve maximum pseudo-likelihood estimation procedure is developed, in which B-splines are used to approximate the nonparametric components of the semiparametric models. This method effectively reduces the original infinite-dimensional estimation problem to a finite-dimensional one. We establish the asymptotic properties of the resulting parameter estimators and conduct extensive simulation studies to evaluate their finite-sample performance. The proposed methodology is applied to the motivating NACC data to investigate potential risk factors for the cumulative incidence of Lewy body dementia.
Authors: Wang X; Wang P; Song X

Title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition.
Abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer's disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.
Authors: Börchers S; Mazzini G; Zetterberg H; Clemmensen C

Title: Validation of plasma biomarker immunoassay-based models for predicting brain amyloid positivity in cognitively impaired individuals.
Abstract: Combining Alzheimer's disease blood biomarkers may improve prediction of amyloid positivity (A+) compared with single biomarkers. Logistic regression models using plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), amyloid beta (Aβ) 42, and Aβ40 were developed in cognitively impaired (CI) participants from Mayo Clinic Rochester (MCR) and validated in Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Mayo Clinic Florida (MCF) cohorts. Performance was measured by area under the curve (AUC) and Probability of Amyloid Positivity Score (PAPS). Plasma p-tau217 alone showed high AUC (95% confidence intervals) across cohorts MCR, 0.928 (0.900-0.953); ADNI, 0.938 (0.915-0.959); MCF, 0.935 (0.893-0.970). Adding Aβ42 to regression models yielded marginal model improvement MCR, 0.940 (0.915-0.963); ADNI, 0.945 (0.922-0.965); MCF, 0.960 (0.925-0.986). Utilization of two cutpoints (≥ 90% sensitivity and specificity), yielded ≤ 10% intermediate results for p-tau217, and ≤ 8% for p-tau217+Aβ42. Addition of Aβ40 did not improve models' performance. An immunoassay-based p-tau217 PAPS model accurately predicted amyloid positivity across independent CI cohorts and achieved confirmatory-test performance with two cutpoints. The added value of Aβ42 was modest and cohort dependent, supporting the potential of use of p-tau217-based PAPS in clinical workflows.
Authors: Syrjanen JA; Figdore DJ; Griswold ME; Wiste HJ; Dierkhising RA; Kremers WK; Lachner C; Graff-Radford NR; Day GS; Graff-Radford J; Jack CR; Knopman DS; Petersen RC; Bornhorst JA; Algeciras-Schimnich A
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Blood-based biomarkers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease: From molecular pathology to therapeutic potential.
Abstract: Alzheimer's (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) represent a major class of neurodegenerative disorders characterized by different proteinopathies with amyloid-β plaques and tau tangles in AD, while α-synuclein containing Lewy bodies in PD, specific molecular signatures. Alongside this central mechanism, they share pathological cascades including axonal degeneration, synaptic dysfunction, glial activation and neuroinflammation. The emergence of blood-based biomarkers, represents a paradigm shift in the field of diagnosis and therapeutics by addressing these core pathological mechanism of central nervous system. This chapter highlights a overview of blood-based biomarkers emerging in the field of AD and PD, exploring the clinical utility of core pathology markers (Aβ42/40, p-tau species, and α-synuclein), alongside other neurodegenerative markers such as neurofilament light chain and glial activation markers like GFAP. Beyond the diagnosis, we emphasize on the potential role of blood-based biomarkers as a surrogate and pharmacodynamic endpoint in disease modifying clinical trial development, facilitating dose optimization and target engagement. Future prospects empathize on the use of multimodal approach integration, trajectory modeling and novel target discovery. Collectively, these blood-based biomarkers enable transition of neurodegenerative disorders treatment from symptom-based classification to towards a mechanism targeted therapeutic framework.
Authors: Priya ; Mittal R; Banerjee J; Dixit A

Title: Understanding Glymphatic's Role In Proteinopathies (GRIP): A single centre case-control study protocol.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) are proteinopathies characterized by pathological accumulation of amyloid beta, phosphorylated-tau, and alpha-synuclein. Impaired clearance of these proteins is thought to contribute to disease pathogenesis, whereas preserved or enhanced clearance may be compensatory. Beyond intracellular degradation within neurons and glial cells, an extracellular clearance pathway, the glymphatic system, facilitates cerebrospinal fluid flow into perivascular spaces, exchange with interstitial fluid, and subsequent clearance from the brain. Glymphatic transport may therefore be critical for removal of excess proteins and metabolic waste, and its dysfunction could promote protein aggregation and neurodegeneration. The Glymphatic's Role In Proteinopathies (GRIP) study is an observational case-control imaging and biomarker study comparing glymphatic clearance in patients with AD, PD, and DLB versus healthy controls. We aim to recruit 70 participants: PD (n = 20), DLB (n = 10), AD (n = 20), and age- and sex-matched healthy controls (n = 20). The AD group will be stratified by pathology, with half amyloid-positive/tau-negative (A + T-) and half amyloid- and tau-positive (A + T+). The PD group will be stratified by disease duration. Participants will undergo baseline MRI followed by intrathecal injection of gadobutrol (0.25 mmol) and serial MRI at 5, 24, 48, and 72 hours. Influx and efflux of tracer will be modeled from T1 signal changes. Blood will be sampled repeatedly from 1 to 72 hours; cerebrospinal fluid will be collected at baseline. Individual glymphatic clearance will be estimated using population pharmacokinetic methods, where gadobutrol serves as a tracer. Sleep will be monitored with triaxial accelerometry and sleep diaries. The primary outcome is group differences in glymphatic clearance metrics between each disease group and controls; secondary analyses will explore associations with cognition, disease severity and duration, sleep quality, and cerebrospinal fluid protein levels.
Authors: Lian SL; Storås TH; Gløersen EM; Løvland G; Hopp E; Mossige I; Hovd M; Uggerud HT; Kardel KR; Bye HA; Buset AL; Valdmanis K; Knapskog AB; Øksengård AR; Fladby T; Nilsen KB; Mardal KA; Ringstad G; Eide PK; Toft M; Nordengen K

Title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins.
Abstract: In Alzheimer's disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation-due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1-disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify the SYK-mTORC1-4E-BP1 signaling axis as a key regulator of microglial mitochondrial biogenesis and immune resolution in AD.
Authors: Bermudez S; Choi JH; Mahmood N; Vogel JW; Almousa H; Huang Z; Kim SH; Zhu VY; Zhou L; Casas-Antillon D; Yaqubi M; Cozachenco D; Stratton JA; Hansson O; Healy L; Aguilar-Valles A; Sonenberg N
Journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

Title: miR‑660‑5p ameliorates neuronal damage in Alzheimer's disease via targeting APP.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system. To investigate miR‑660‑5p expression among patients with AD and explore the molecular mechanism underlying its regulation of AD‑related pathological progression. A total of 86 AD patients and 86 healthy controls were enrolled. Serum miR‑660‑5p was detected by real‑time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Inflammatory factors were measured via enzyme‑linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). SH‑SY5Y cells were treated with aggregated Aβ₁‑₄₂ preparation to establish an in‑vitro AD‑like injury model. Serum miR‑660‑5p was significantly downregulated in AD patients (P < 0.001), positively correlated with Mini‑Mental State Examination (MMSE, r = 0.684) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA, r = 0.640) scores, and negatively correlated with serum interleukin‑6 (IL‑6, r = - 0.658) and tumor necrosis factor‑α (TNF‑α, r = - 0.614). Receiver‑operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis for AD yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.873. Mechanistically, miR‑660‑5p targets and inhibits APP expression to mitigate Aβ‑induced neuronal injury and neuroinflammation. miR-660-5p is downregulated in patients with AD. It mitigates aggregated Aβ₁-₄₂ preparation‑triggered neuronal damage and neuroinflammation in vitro by targeted inhibition of APP expression.
Authors: Gong P; Su X; Fang Y

Title: Cerebrospinal fluid surfactant protein-G in neurodegenerative dementia: A comparative study with idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus.
Abstract: BackgroundSurfactant protein G (SP-G) is a recently characterized protein potentially involved in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics. Its role in human neurodegenerative dementia remains unknown.ObjectiveTo investigate the potential clinical relevance of CSF SP-G levels in neurodegenerative dementia (ND; including Alzheimer's disease [AD] and frontotemporal dementia [FTD]), idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), vascular dementia (VaD), and clinical controls (CTR).MethodsCSF SP-G levels were quantified in 94 individuals: 35 with ND (11 AD + 24 FTD), 19 with iNPH, 13 with VaD, and 27 CTR. Group differences were analyzed using ANOVA with post hoc tests. ANCOVA was performed to adjust for age.ResultsCSF SP-G levels differed significantly among groups in the primary analysis (ANOVA: F(3,90) = 3.862, p = 0.012), with higher levels in iNPH compared with ND (p = 0.012) and CTR (p = 0.026). No significant differences were observed between ND, VaD, and CTR groups. After adjustment for age, the group effect was no longer significant (F(3,89) = 2.253, p = 0.088).ConclusionsThis is the first study to investigate CSF SP-G levels in neurodegenerative dementia. Our findings suggest that SP-G is more closely related to altered CSF physiology in iNPH than to neurodegenerative pathology, although the influence of age indicates that these observations should be interpreted with caution. SP-G may represent a candidate marker of CSF homeostasis and fluid dynamics. Larger, age-matched studies integrating SP-G with established CSF biomarkers and neuroimaging are needed to clarify its diagnostic and pathophysiological significance.
Authors: Cattaldo S; Scarpina F; Prina E; Piterà P; Milesi A; Sabattini E; Bigoni M; Azzaro C; Pradotto LG; Mauro A; Priano L

Title: A narrative review of rare variants in Alzheimer's disease: diverse populations inform diverse mechanisms.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) heritability is estimated to be 58-79%. However, much is yet to be explained. Rare variation is one potential source of missing heritability in complex traits. We reviewed the studies that first identified rare variants associated with AD, comparing the characteristics of their samples (comparing studies focusing on "restricted" populations vs. studies from multiple populations) and reviewing what biological processes and molecular mechanisms they may support. We conducted a review of rare variant association studies in AD, identifying 64 variants across 39 genes (ABCA7, AC099552.4, ACER3, ADAM17, AKAP9, APP, APOE, API5, ASRGL1/TUT1, ATP8B4, BIN1, C15ORF41/CDIN1, CASP7, CASP8, CD2AP, COBL, COL4A1, CR1, CST3, EPHA1, FUS, IGF1R/ARRDC4, LINC00298, MYRF, NCK2, NOTCH3, PIK3C2G, PLD3, PLCG2, PLXNC1, PTK2B, RAB3B, SORL1, SPOCK3/ANXA10, TCIRG1, TREM2, UNC5C, WASHC5). There is an overrepresentation of genes related with amyloid-beta, phagocytosis, apoptotic cells engulfment, membrane invagination and cellular component organization. Thirty (45.5%) studies were performed in "restricted" discovery populations. These had lower number of cases and lower MAF on cases than the studies from multiple populations. Studies in populations from a restricted ancestry or region of collection have been fruitful in revealing rare variants associated with disease. Diverse backgrounds have revealed different variants - some genes have only been implicated in AD by the identification of rare variants in these populations. Enrichment analyses of associated genes revealed overrepresentation in biological processes related to amyloid-beta metabolism, phagocytosis and engulfment of apoptotic cells, regulation of cell migration and cell component organization, locomotion, and immune related responses. These results highlight the importance of diverse but focused genetic studies.
Authors: Tábuas-Pereira M; Santana I; Kun-Rodrigues C; Paquette K; Brás J; Guerreiro R
Journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

Title: Molecular Neuroimaging in Alzheimer's Disease.
Abstract: Molecular neuroimaging in Alzheimer's disease has shifted from a confirmatory diagnostic adjunct to a decision-defining clinical tool that informs diagnosis, treatment eligibility, and longitudinal therapeutic monitoring. Driven by global therapeutic approvals of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies and high-precision fluid biomarkers, molecular imaging now adjudicates diagnostic certainty and governs progression to disease-modifying therapy. While high-precision plasma biomarkers increasingly serve as scalable screening tools, they frequently require adjudication by amyloid or tau PET to resolve indeterminate results and enable treatment decisions. 18F-FDG PET remains an important diagnostic tool for patients with more advanced dementia presenting with complex syndromes.
Authors: Verma Saluja K; Jindal S; Benzinger TLS

Title: Emerging and Repurposed Immune System Modulators for Alzheimer's Disease.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains an incurable neurodegenerative condition to date. Pathologically, the hallmarks of AD are (i) extracellular senile plaques mainly composed of amyloid beta peptides (Aβ), (ii) intracellular neurofibrillary tangles comprised of abnormally folded and hyperphosphorylated tau proteins, and (iii) neuroinflammation. In the past two decades, the investigation of these brain pathologies has led to the identification of novel diagnostic biomarkers and putative therapeutic targets, ultimately resulting in the first two commercial disease-modifying anti-Aβ immunotherapies. More recently, modulation of the overactivated central immune system has emerged as a unique putative approach to slow down the progression of AD. In the present narrative review, we summarize the main findings on modulators of inflammation tested in Phase 2 and 3 trials in AD patients. After a deep literature review, we ended up selecting 19 agents spanning immune primers, monoclonal antibodies, recombinant proteins, synthetic peptides, immunomodulatory drugs, ion channel blockers, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, senolytics, antivirals, and herbal formulations. For each agent, we briefly explain the preclinical findings that led to translation into clinical trials and provide details about each trial design, and, when available, the main findings from the trials. Overall, it appears that Aβ and abnormal tau activate both the innate and adaptive immune systems, which in turn galvanize the production of Aβ and abnormal tau, thereby forming a viscous cycle that inflates AD neuropathology and is difficult to interrupt. Based on the successes and failures of the 19 agents reported here, we postulate that immune system modulators with the strongest potential for AD treatment are those displaying pleiotropic actions on both innate and adaptive immune responses rather than those exhibiting very targeted mechanisms. We conclude that modulators of inflammation need to be studied further, both as stand-alone AD therapies and in combination with anti-amyloid and anti-tau approaches.
Authors: Decourt B; Azarfar K; Reyna EM; Kennedy JM; Sabbagh MN

Title: A Data-Driven Operational Definition of Square-Wave Jerks and Its Diagnostic Utility in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy.
Abstract: The Movement Disorder Society diagnostic criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) list frequent square-wave jerks (SWJ) as a suggestive oculomotor feature. A standardised operational definition of SWJ is however presently lacking. To create a data-driven optimal SWJ definition and to assess its diagnostic utility in PSP. We prospectively recruited PSP n = 25, Parkinson's disease (PD) n = 32, Alzheimer's disease (AD) n = 35, and controls n = 88. SWJ were recorded with a visual fixation task using video-oculography. Multiple candidate definitions of SWJ were generated by systematically varying morphological features, producing 32 candidate definitions. A nested cross-validation was used to obtain unbiased diagnostic performance and optimised SWJ definition. Results were then externally tested in a fully independent sample of n = 25 PSP, n = 41 PD and n = 25 controls. The optimal selected SWJ definition consisted of saccade amplitude 1°-8°, intra-SWJ intervals 20-600 ms, directional opposition within ±45°, and amplitude similarity ≤ 0.25. Only SWJ rate, and not morphological features, was distinctive for PSP. SWJ rate gave out-of-fold AUCs of 0.81 for PSP versus controls, 0.71 for PSP versus AD, 0.63 for PSP versus PD, and 0.76 for PSP versus all non-PSP groups. Post hoc analyses using this data-driven definition on the external validation cohort yielded relatively comparable results. SWJ rate > 24/min had high specificity, but low sensitivity, for PSP when compared with PD. SWJ rate was significantly increased in PSP but with insufficient discriminant ability for use as a stand-alone diagnostic marker. This data-driven definition may serve as a reproducible operational definition for future research.
Authors: Nguyen DD; Quattrone A; Paine M; Fazlollahi A; Lee S; Wang BB; Davidson T; Coleman F; O'Sullivan JD; Nestor PJ

Title: Multiscale organization of amyloid-associated vulnerability across the hippocampal memory system.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) selectively affects interconnected components of the hippocampal memory system, yet most MRI biomarkers characterize neurodegeneration using whole-hippocampal or isolated regional measurements. We tested whether amyloid-associated structural vulnerability is selectively concentrated in the cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) and the dentate gyrus (DG), reproducible across independent 1Florida ADRC and ADNI cohorts, and spatially localized within these subfields. We integrated hippocampal subfield volumetry, covariate-adjusted amyloid-associated vulnerability scores, 10,000-resample bootstrap rank-stability analysis, complementary cross-sectional clinical-stage comparisons, exploratory diffusion MRI, and within-subfield occupancy mapping. The cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) region and the dentate gyrus (DG) retained the two highest covariate-adjusted amyloid-associated point rankings in both cohorts. In ADRC, the adjusted scores were 5.06% for CA1 and 4.38% for DG, with bootstrap Top-2 frequencies of 59.02% and 41.44%, respectively; in ADNI, the adjusted scores were 9.10% for CA1 and 9.37% for DG, with Top-2 frequencies of 73.60% and 76.40%, respectively. Bootstrap resampling quantified uncertainty in regional scores and rank positions and supported recurrent top two placement of CA1 and DG, while also demonstrating overlap in uncertainty among several ROIs. Complementary cross-sectional comparisons described CA1 and DG volume differences across clinical stages in ADRC and ADNI. Exploratory diffusion MRI identified effect-size differences in hippocampal-associated pathways, but none of the 20 region-metric comparisons survived Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. Collectively, these findings support a reproducible cross-sectional pattern of amyloid-associated vulnerability within the hippocampal memory system, centered on CA1 and DG and accompanied by spatially heterogeneous within-subfield structural loss. The diffusion MRI findings are exploratory and provide anatomical context rather than evidence of temporal ordering. Longitudinal studies are required to determine the sequence in which these abnormalities emerge.
Authors: Cui X; Yan Liang T; Adeyosoye M; Ezzati M; Simkhada B; Cabrerizo M; Curiel Cid R; Rosselli M; Barreto A; Rishe ND; Loewenstein DA; Adjouadi M

Title: Deubiquitinating Enzymes in Alzheimer's Disease: From Protein Homeostasis to Diverse Pathological Processes.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder involving multiple pathological processes, including amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, tau pathology, impaired autophagy, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and synaptic dysfunction. Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) reverse ubiquitination and regulate protein stability, degradation, and cellular signaling. Although studies of DUBs in AD have largely focused on Aβ metabolism and tau homeostasis, accumulating evidence implicates DUBs in a broader range of AD-related processes, including autophagy, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial function, and synaptic function. Several DUBs have also been implicated in more than one of these processes, although these effects have often been identified in different experimental models. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of DUBs in major AD-related pathological processes and discuss the mechanisms through which individual DUBs may influence different aspects of AD pathology. We also discuss the limitations of current studies and the potential and challenges of targeting DUBs in AD.
Authors: Shi X; Chen G; Wang X; Ma R; Li G

Title: Vascular drivers of cerebrospinal fluid movement and enlarged perivascular spaces.
Abstract: Perivascular spaces (PVSs) facilitate cerebrospinal fluid flow and waste clearance, which are critical for maintaining brain homeostasis. Enlarged PVSs (ePVSs) are an emerging marker of cerebral small vessel disease and are implicated in protein accumulation, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline. While prior reviews have described the anatomy and correlates of ePVSs, the vascular mechanisms that drive perivascular fluid dynamics, and how their dysfunction might lead to ePVSs, have not been reviewed. This review examines how vascular mechanisms drive perivascular fluid dynamics and discusses how their impairment may contribute to ePVS formation and their impact on cognition. We propose an integrated vascular-ePVS hypothesis in which early vascular dysfunction may contribute to impaired waste clearance and ePVS burden, potentially linking early-life vascular health with later proteinopathy and cognitive decline. Elucidating the vascular contributions to ePVSs is imperative to identify therapeutic targets to preserve cognition in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.
Authors: LeFevre JD; Vyas Y; Jefferson AL
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Vasomechanic treatment is associated with increased efflux of human brain proteins.
Abstract: An age-related neurovascular impairment in nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation and reciprocal Piezo1-dependent vascular vasoconstriction may precede the accumulation of soluble brain proteins such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and disruption of brain fluid homeostasis in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Preclinical studies suggest that restoring these pathways can enhance neurofluid transport and improve cognitive outcomes. In this study (EudraCT 2021-000625-27), we investigated the effects of sublingual NO and Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibrations (WBV<sub>p</sub>) in healthy adults (n = 29) using multimodal neuroimaging and blood biomarker analysis. The combined intervention (NO+WBV<sub>p</sub>) was associated with correlating changes in brain fluid dynamics and increased blood levels of soluble brain-derived proteins (Aβ<sub>40&42</sub>, GFAP). These effects increased with age and the magnitude of NO-induced hypotension. The interventions were well tolerated under controlled experimental conditions. Overall, the findings are consistent with transient redistribution of brain-derived proteins toward circulation, suggesting a potential non-invasive approach to increase neurofluidic solute efflux in humans. Pre-specified primary endpoints, changes in circulating brain-derived protein concentrations, brain fluid imaging and brain pulsation measures, were met. Secondary outcomes included physiological analyses.
Authors: Tuunanen J; Hautamäki K; Väyrynen T; Järvelä M; Korhonen V; Huotari N; Kaakinen M; Kananen J; Helakari H; Raitamaa L; Jukkola J; Herukka SK; Laurén K; Salmi U; Eklund L; Nikkinen J; Nedergaard M; Kiviniemi V

Title: Protocatechuic acid alleviates the progression of Alzheimer's disease by regulating p53/GADD45/MAPK signaling pathway.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide lacking effective treatments. Protocatechuic acid (PCA), a natural polyphenol found in various foods and medicinal herbs, exhibits diverse bioactivities; but its role in AD remains unclear. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of PCA. In vitro, PCA significantly attenuated glutamic-induced cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, calcium influx, and apoptosis in PC12, SH-SY5Y, and HT22 cells. In vivo, PCA improved cognitive performance in the Morris water maze, open field, and novel object recognition tests in a d-galactose/AlCl₃-induced AD mice, and mitigated hippocampal and cortical histopathological damage. Integrated transcriptomic and network pharmacology analyses identified the apoptosis, p53, and MAPK as key pathways. RT-qPCR and western blot analyses revealed that PCA downregulated p53, GADD45B, GADD45G, and phosphorylated p38. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PCA alleviates AD progression by inhibiting the p53/GADD45/MAPK axis, positioning it as a promising natural candidate for AD prevention.
Authors: Wang J; Tu X; Yang R; Kang J; Gu A; Han B; Kai G

Title: On the Need to Revise the Amyloid Cascade Hypothesis.
Abstract: Seven million people in the USA are estimated to suffer from Alzheimer's disease (AD), a number expected to double by 2050. Patient care costs >$350 billion/year now but will exceed $1 trillion by 2050, bankrupting our economy. Tremendous progress in understanding and treating AD has been made over the past 4 decades, yet, after >400 clinical trials, no efficacious AD treatments exist. The amyloid cascade hypothesis (ACH), the leading disease model, holds that amyloid β (Aβ) initiates a cascade leading to disease. Alternative processing cleaves APP in the middle of Aβ, producing the C-terminal fragment, p3. Simply put, if the ACH is true, no Aβ means no disease because p3 is believed soluble, non-amyloidogenic, and nontoxic. However, recent studies have shown this to be untrue. In fact, p3 is more amyloidogenic than Aβ, and is neurotoxic. It also forms mixed aggregates with Aβ that have distinct structures and neurotoxicities. ACH has led the AD field to largely ignore these facts. Here, we provide an integrated perspective on how this has come about and urge expansion of the ACH to consider the possible roles of p3 in AD and to refer to it as Amyloid α (Aα), to better reflect its nature.
Authors: Teplow DB; Raskatov JA
Journal: Chembiochem : a European journal of chemical biology

Title: Operant House: A versatile open-source platform for automated operant conditioning testing of mice in home cages.
Abstract: Operant conditioning is a powerful method for probing cognitive functions, yet its widespread use is constrained by low throughput, labor-intensive procedures, and high costs. Here, we developed "Operant House," a low-cost, programmable device equipped with a touchscreen, retractable levers, and a water-reward port, designed to enable automated operant conditioning with minimal experimenter intervention in individually housed mice within their home cages. Although individual home-cage testing requires careful attention to animal welfare, the system permits continuous monitoring through live camera observation and recorded videos. As proof of concept, we implemented two cognitive protocols: a delayed non-match-to-position (DNMTP) test for assessing working memory and a two-choice spatial discrimination (TCSD) test involving working-memory-related processes and behavioral flexibility. Because working memory impairment is one of the earliest clinical features of Alzheimer's disease (AD), we further applied these protocols to a knock-in mouse model carrying familial AD-associated amyloid precursor protein mutations (AppNL-G-F mice). Using this model, we detected significant working memory deficits as early as 5 months of age. At this age, we also detected subtle and spatially heterogeneous synaptic alterations in the prefrontal cortex, whereas conventional electrophysiological measures were largely preserved. Together, these findings highlight the Operant House as a cost-effective, scalable platform for assessing higher cognitive functions in mice, offering an accessible tool for investigating neurological and neuropsychiatric disease models.
Authors: Otsuka S; Nakamura Y; Ito-Ishida A; Suzuki K; Ishikawa A; Matsuda K; Suyama S; Contractor A; Yuzaki M

Title: Proteomics Reveals Blood-Brain Barrier Membrane Protein Remodeling in Amyloid-β Pathology.
Abstract: The protective function of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is achieved by membrane proteins expressed in the endothelial cells of brain microvessels, such as tight junction proteins, receptors, and transporters, which regulate the passage of solutes, including nutrients, drugs, and metabolites. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques, BBB dysfunction has been widely reported. However, quantitative information on Aβ-associated changes in the membrane proteome in the brain microvasculature remains limited. Here, we investigated the changes in abundances of membrane proteins playing roles in BBB function in the isolated brain microvessels of a mouse model mimicking human Aβ pathology, 5xFAD mice, versus corresponding wild-type (WT) mice using a state-of-the-art liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based data-independent acquisition (DIA) quantitative proteomics. In addition, we applied quantitative targeted absolute proteomics to evaluate the impact of Aβ1-42 on the absolute protein abundance of multiple transporters in an in vitro model of brain endothelial cells, hCMEC/D3. We identified changes in the protein abundance of numerous proteins involved in BBB integrity, including tight junction-associated proteins and proteins implicated in Aβ transport and clearance, in the brain microvasculature of 5xFAD mice. Furthermore, Aβ1-42 treatment altered GLUT1 protein abundance and the gene expression of SLC27A1 and SLC22A2 in hCMEC/D3 cells, which play roles in nutrient transport and drug disposition at the BBB. The present study provides novel insights into Aβ-associated molecular alterations in brain microvascular membrane proteins and advances our understanding of BBB changes in AD. The results may support the development of BBB-targeted therapeutic approaches and strategies for optimizing brain drug delivery in AD.
Authors: Hyvärinen J; Todorovska R; Palacios MDP; Gynther M; Afonin A; Lehtonen M; Auriola S; Saveleva L; Kanninen KM; Fricker G; Puris E

Title: Novel pyrimidine-based N-Acylhydrazones as dual AChE inhibitors and antioxidants targeting Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cholinergic dysfunction and oxidative stress, making the development of multi-target-directed ligands (MTDLs) an attractive therapeutic strategy. Herein, we designed and synthesized a novel series of pyrimidinone-based acyl hydrazones 6a-g bearing substituted aryl or heteroaryl (furan) moieties. The synthesized compounds were evaluated for their in vitro acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitory and antioxidant activities. The synthesized pyrimidinone-based acyl hydrazones (6a-g) exhibited promising acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitory activity. Compound 6 g emerged as the most potent inhibitor, with an IC₅₀ value of 4.79 μM, corresponding to approximately 55.7-fold greater potency than tacrine hydrochloride (IC₅₀ = 266 μM) under standardized parallel assay conditions. Compounds 6a, 6b, and 6f also demonstrated potent AChE inhibition, with IC₅₀ values ranging from 15.9 to 128.65 μM, whereas the remaining derivatives exhibited moderate to weak inhibitory activity. The synthesized compounds also displayed promising antioxidant activity in DPPH and nitric oxide (NO) radical scavenging assays. Notably, 6g exhibit potent DPPH and nitric oxide radical scavenging activity, surpassing standard antioxidant (ascorbic acid) by approximately 35-fold and 9-fold, respectively. Molecular docking studies supported the experimental results by revealing favorable binding modes of the most active compounds within the AChE active site, while suggesting potential computationally predicted interactions with BuChE, 5-LOX, and COX-2. Furthermore, in silico drug-likeness and ADME analyses provided baseline pharmacokinetic profiles, guiding rational structural optimization strategies to enhance blood-brain barrier permeability. These findings identify pyrimidinone-based acyl hydrazones as promising multifunctional lead compounds for the development of novel therapeutic agents against Alzheimer's neurocognitive disorder.
Authors: Abd Al Moaty MN; Moustafa A; Hegazy AS; Sobhy AA; Ghareeb DA; Awad LF; Ibrahim NA

Title: [Lead exposure aggravates Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>-induced microglial activation through mitochondrial calcium uniporter-mediated mitochondrial calcium accumulation].
Abstract: To investigate the role of mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) in lead (Pb)‑potentiated microglial activation induced by amyloid β‑protein (1-42) (Aβ1-42) and the regulatory mechanism by which Pb exacerbates Alzheimer disease (AD)-like pathology. Cultured BV2 cells treated with 10 μmol/L Aβ<sub>1-42</sub> for 12 h (Aβ<sub>1-42</sub> group), 10 μmol/L Pb for 12 h (Pb group), or 10 μmol/L Aβ<sub>1-42</sub> for 1 h followed by 10 μmol/L Pb for 12 h (Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>+Pb group) were examined for changes in intracellular calcium levels using ICP-MS. Morphological changes of the treated cells were observed, and iNOS release and oxidative stress were assessed with immunofluorescence staining. The changes in cellular MCU protein expression was determined with Western blotting, and cell viability was evaluated using CCK-8 assay. Compared with Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>-treated cells, the cells with the combined treatment showed significantly elevated mitochondrial Ca²⁺ content and increased MCU protein expression. Downregulation of MCU expression obviously alleviated the reduction of viability of HT22 cells treated with the supernatant from BV2 cells co-treated with Pb and Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>. The combined treatment with lead and Aβ<sub>1-42</sub> caused activation of BV2 cells, manifested by increased cell volume and number of protrusions and intensified fluorescence signals of both Iba1 and iNOS. Downregulation of MCU expression significantly suppressed activation of BV2 cells in the siMCU+Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>+Pb group, and obviously lowered oxidative stress level, mitochondrial calcium overload, and membrane potential level in the cells. Pb exposure exacerbates neuronal injury mediated by Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>-activated microglia through upregulation of MCU expression, which causes mitochondrial calcium accumulation to trigger oxidative stress.
Authors: Chen L; Long Y; Huang D; Zheng G; Meng X
Journal: Nan fang yi ke da xue xue bao = Journal of Southern Medical University

Title: CD8<sup>+</sup> t cell-mediated regulation of synaptic integrity in Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) has traditionally been interpreted through amyloid, tau, and innate immune frameworks, with the complement cascade long regarded as the principal driver of aberrant synaptic pruning. Synaptic loss is increasingly recognized as one of the strongest correlates of cognitive decline. This review examines an emerging CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell-synapse axis that extends beyond complement-centric models. We discuss how brain-infiltrating CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells intersect with synaptic integrity through MHC-I-dependent and MHC-I-independent mechanisms, including IFN-γ-mediated microglial reprogramming and granzyme K-driven non-canonical complement activation. Early effector-like subsets may promote neuroinflammation and synaptic injury, whereas later tissue-resident or regulatory populations can exert protective functions by gating microglial states. The net outcome depends on disease stage, antigenic milieu, anatomical niche, and microglial context. We emphasize that direct antigen-specific, MHC-I-restricted synaptic attack remains unproven in human AD, and that observed T-cell infiltration may reflect reverse causality. Translational limitations across species are evaluated, and we outline subset-specific immunomodulation, ApoE4-stratified strategies, and biomarker-guided trial designs as future directions. Overall, CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells are positioned not as uniform cytotoxic executors, but as dynamic, context-dependent regulators of synaptic outcomes in AD.
Authors: Fu H; Yang J; Zhang M

Title: Golgi dysfunction in Alzheimer disease: from human multiomic signatures to therapeutic targets.
Abstract: Deciphering the intricate pathogenesis of Alzheimer disease (AD) has been a highly demanding task for researchers for decades. Evidence from from human multiomic studies provides critical insights into complex disease mechanisms and drives novel findings. However, the data are often selectively comprehended, leaving a few notable factors underappreciated in the research field. We focus on the Golgi apparatus, one of the most undervalued organelles in AD research, to demonstrate its multidimensional contribution to the pathogenesis. Given the importance of Golgi in modulating intracellular protein and lipid homeostasis, implication of Golgi in AD pathogenesis deserves thorough investigation. In this review, we describe changes in Golgi morphology and function in AD, and summarize specific Golgi-related factors discovered by genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and lipidomic data using human samples. Based on the findings, we demonstrate mechanistic link of Golgi-related factors to AD pathogenesis and highlight potential therapeutic strategies to modify Golgi-mediated pathogenesis. Overall, Golgi dysfunction may serve as a notable mechanistic hub of AD pathogenesis, making it a promising target for development of novel therapeutic strategies.
Authors: Song J; Lee SJ; Mook-Jung I

Title: Brain microstructure mediates the relationship between Alzheimer's proteinopathies and memory.
Abstract: We examined how amyloid beta (Aβ) and tau accumulation affected gray matter (GM) microstructural integrity and how such alterations impacted memory. We tested voxel-wise mediation models to examine the relationships between (1) positron emission tomography-derived Aβ and tau accumulation and GM microstructural integrity assessed with neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging, (2) GM microstructural integrity and memory controlling for Aβ and tau, and (3) the indirect effect of Aβ and tau on memory through GM microstructural integrity in 194 participants with memory impairments. Tau had a greater impact on GM microstructure than did Aβ. GM microstructural alterations in posterior cortical regions were associated with worse memory when controlling for Alzheimer's proteinopathies. GM microstructural alterations mediated the relationship between Alzheimer's proteinopathies and memory. GM microstructural alterations have functional ramifications given their mediating effect on the relationship between Alzheimer's proteinopathies and memory and their association with worse memory beyond Alzheimer's proteinopathies.
Authors: Devignes Q; Pruitt PJ; Petscavage K; Koeppe RA; Albin RL; Peltier SJ; Rahman-Filipiak A; Giordani B; Iordan AD; Hampstead BM
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Alzheimer's disease and olfactory dysfunction: A 20-year systematic bibliometric and genomic analysis.
Abstract: With the acceleration of global population aging, early diagnosis and intervention of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative disorders have become major public health challenges. Olfactory dysfunction (OD) is increasingly recognized as one of the earliest clinical manifestations of AD, highlighting the importance of understanding the relationship between AD and olfactory impairment. This study integrates bibliometric analysis and genomic approaches to systematically characterize global research trends and explore potential molecular mechanisms underlying AD and OD from 2006 to 2025. Publications related to AD and OD were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, and bibliometric analyses were performed using CiteSpace and VOSviewer, with results further validated through the Scopus database. A total of 1412 publications were identified, demonstrating sustained growth over the past two decades and a rapid expansion phase after 2019. The United States and China were the leading contributors in publication output and international collaboration, although research development remained geographically uneven. Keyword analysis revealed a gradual transition from behavioral and pathological investigations toward early diagnosis, biomarker discovery, therapeutic exploration, and advanced technologies. Genomic analysis identified 1838 shared genes between AD and OD, with key hub genes including AKT1, INS, and ALB involved in common biological pathways associated with neuronal function, cognitive regulation, and olfactory system homeostasis. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the evolving research landscape of AD and OD, identifies emerging trends and potential molecular targets, and offers valuable insights for early screening, mechanistic investigation, and translational research in neurodegenerative diseases.
Authors: Yang G; Meng C; Zhu D

Title: Efficacy and safety of aducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab in Alzheimer's disease: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Abstract: BackgroundAnti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies offer a treatment strategy for early Alzheimer's disease, but their modest efficacy must be weighed against important safety concerns.ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of aducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab in randomized placebo-controlled trials.MethodsPubMed, Cochrane, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched through February 2026 for randomized placebo-controlled trials evaluating aducanumab, lecanemab, or donanemab in early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. Outcomes included Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), amyloid-related imaging abnormalities-edema/effusion (ARIA-E), amyloid-related imaging abnormalities-hemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H), and APOE ε4-stratified ARIA-E. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed.ResultsSeven trials were included. Treatment favored intervention for ADAS-Cog (SMD -0.15, 95% CI -0.21 to -0.10), CDR-SB (MD -0.41, 95% CI -0.63 to -0.18), and MMSE (MD 0.44, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.86), although effects were small. Treatment increased ARIA-E (23.9% versus 1.9%; RR 11.65, 95% CI 9.06 to 14.99) and ARIA-H (16.8% versus 6.8%; RR 2.45, 95% CI 1.94 to 3.09). Among treated participants with APOE ε4-stratified ARIA-E data, APOE ε4 carriers had higher ARIA-E risk than non-carriers (29.3% versus 13.8%; RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.67 to 2.64). Brain-volume loss, ventricular enlargement, and treatment-related deaths were narratively identified but not pooled.ConclusionsAducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab showed statistically significant but small slowing of decline that may not reach patient-perceptible clinical meaningfulness. Increased ARIA risk and additional safety signals support cautious selection, imaging surveillance, and individualized risk-benefit discussions.
Authors: Ali M; Shabbir H; Shaharyar M; Mukesh S; Rodriguez A; Afshani M; Kalra D; Koriesh A

Title: Sphingolipid and ceramide associations with tau pathology vary across diverse ethnoracial groups in postmortem brain tissue.
Abstract: Metabolic dysregulation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), with numerous studies characterizing metabolic pathways associated with AD onset and progression. A limitation of these studies has been a focus on non-Hispanic white participants. Despite evidence that AD prevalence, progression, and biomarkers differ across ethnoracial groups, it remains unclear whether previously identified metabolic dysregulation in AD brains generalizes across populations. We analyzed metabolomics data from 547 postmortem brain tissue samples of Hispanic American, Non-Hispanic African American, and White subjects, providing the largest multiethnic AD brain cohort to date. A metabolome-wide association study examined how relationships between metabolite abundance and AD neuropathology varied by ethnoracial group. Forty-eight metabolites exhibited significant heterogeneity with tau pathology (Braak stage), with enrichment in tricarboxylic-acid-cycle intermediates and sphingolipid-ceramide pathway lipids, and with metabolite-tau associations driven predominantly by the Hispanic American and non-Hispanic White groups. These findings reveal ethnoracial-specific metabolic signatures of tau pathology and emphasize the need to evaluate emerging therapeutic targets across diverse groups.
Authors: Schweickart A; Batra R; Huynh K; Blach C; Kueider-Paisley A; Reddy JS; Bennett DA; Meikle PJ; Zhang B; De Jager PL; Heath L; Beck J; Scanlan J; Seyfried NT; Dickson DW; Ertekin-Taner N; Kaddurah-Daouk R; Arnold M; Krumsiek J
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Accelerated clinical evaluations for Alzheimer's disease: feasibility across specialty and rural care settings.
