Abstract: Timely diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly important given the availability of disease-modifying therapies, yet current diagnostic pathways remain fragmented, resource-intensive, and difficult to access. We developed the accelerated clinical evaluation for Alzheimer's disease (ACE-AD), a nursing-led workflow integrating a clinical interview, cognitive testing, blood biomarkers, and portable magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to streamline dementia evaluation. ACE-AD was evaluated in two phases. Phase 1 validated the workflow in 20 participants with standard-of-care (SOC) memory clinic diagnoses compared against ACE-AD-derived etiologic diagnosis, cognitive staging, and neuroimaging findings. Phase 2 adapted the workflow for a rural neurology practice, assessing feasibility, utility, and acceptability. In Phase 1 (n = 20), primary etiologic diagnoses were universally concordant between SOC and ACE-AD evaluations, with 90% agreement on AD as a primary or contributing etiology. Cognitive stage agreed in 13 participants (65%); ACE-AD rated all discordant cases as less impaired. Portable MRI identified clinically relevant abnormalities consistent with SOC MRI, and patients, care partners, and clinicians rated the workflow highly acceptable. In Phase 2 (n = 7), the rural neurologist reported improved diagnostic confidence, efficiency, treatment planning, and patient communication without workflow disruption. A structured, nursing-led evaluation integrating blood biomarkers and portable MRI can capture sufficient clinical information to support specialist dementia diagnosis while shifting much of the diagnostic workup earlier in the care pathway. These findings support further evaluation of ACE-AD as a scalable approach for expanding access to timely dementia diagnosis in both specialty and resource-limited settings.
Authors: Vidoni ED; Morris JK; Weis K; Townley RA; Parks AC; Brunette AM; Gillen LR; Fikru SA; Montero A; Brubaker R; Woodall D; Agee S; Summers K; Levendovszky SR; Davis D; Woodward JL; Burns JM
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Disrupted synaptic vacuolar H+-ATPase renders synaptic vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease.
Abstract: Defective synaptic transmission is a prominent pathology that underlies cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's disease (AD), highlighting the need to elucidate molecular mechanisms of synaptic failure. Vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase), a proton-pumping enzyme, is essential for synaptic vesicle acidification and neurotransmitter loading. However, whether SV-associated V-ATPase is vulnerable to AD remains unclear. Here, using SV-rich fractions from postmortem brain tissues, we identified SV-associated V-ATPase deficits, including decreased enzymatic activity, impaired complex assembly, and altered expression of its key subunits in AD. SV-associated V-ATPase dysfunction was further associated with pathological and clinical characteristics of AD. Genetic downregulation of the V-ATPase V1D subunit, a component reduced in AD brains, disrupted V-ATPase proton transport and impaired SV acidification. Further experiments using 5×FAD mice, which exhibited AD-like SV-associated V-ATPase deficits, demonstrated the deleterious impact of V-ATPase dysfunction on SV acidification and synaptic transmission including presynaptic neurotransmitter release. In addition, ex vivo studies identified amyloid β-induced oxidative stress as a driver of V1D loss and V-ATPase disassembly, linking AD pathology to SV-associated V-ATPase dysfunction. These findings indicate that SV-associated V-ATPase dysfunction contributes to synaptic failure and cognitive deficits in AD. Therapeutic avenues to mitigate V-ATPase dysfunction have the potential to attenuate synaptic failure for the management of AD.
Authors: Chen Y; Emam KAF; Yue S; Tian J; Wang T; Park A; Mishra S; Deep G; Wang ZJ; Du H; Guo L

Title: EP2 and EP4 in Alzheimer's Disease: Cell-Dependent Signalling and Implications for Selective Targeting.
Abstract: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE<sub>2</sub>) signalling influences amyloid-β (Aβ) processing, myeloid function, and neuronal injury in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although EP2 and EP4 share Gs-cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signalling, their cellular effects differ. This review integrates genetic, pharmacological, ageing, and AD-model evidence to assess receptor-selective targeting. EP2 deletion enhances myeloid Aβ handling and reduces microglia-mediated neuronal injury in experimental systems, providing a rationale for selective EP2 inhibition. In aged mice, PGE<sub>2</sub>-EP2 signalling redirects glucose towards glycogen storage and restricts myeloid mitochondrial respiration; benefits from a predominantly peripheral antagonist suggest that some age-related outcomes may improve without high brain exposure. Chronic antagonist studies in AD models, however, show variable effects on inflammation, amyloid burden, and behaviour. EP4 exhibits contrasting cell-dependent actions: activation supports microglial Aβ uptake and inflammatory control, whereas signalling in some amyloid precursor protein (APP)-expressing cells promotes APP internalisation and Aβ production. Human AD evidence remains mainly tissue-based; EP2 antagonist testing has involved healthy volunteers, not patients with AD. These findings indicate that receptor selectivity alone is insufficient to predict therapeutic outcomes. Further studies should combine cell-specific receptor manipulation, measurements of central and peripheral exposure, and separate assessments of Aβ production, clearance, tissue injury, and functional outcomes.
Authors: Zhao X; Zeng Y; Song Z; He J; He Q; Lin H; Liu L; Yu W; Cheng S

Title: Cyclic Peptides Target CAPON and Modulate Cellular Responses under Alzheimer's Disease-Relevant Stress.
Abstract: CAPON (NOS1AP) is an adaptor protein involved in neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) signaling and has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), excitotoxicity, and tau-associated neurodegeneration. Here, we report the identification of cyclic peptide ligands targeting CAPON using phage display screening of a disulfide-constrained peptide library. Phage enrichment, ELISA validation, microscale thermophoresis (MST), and biolayer interferometry (BLI) identified CAP1 as the lead peptide, exhibiting low micromolar binding affinity toward CAPON. Computational studies further supported stable CAPON-CAP1 interactions through complementary hydrophobic and electrostatic contacts. Functionally, CAP1 attenuated Aβ42-induced neuronal toxicity, suppressed NMDA-driven nitric oxide production, and reduced AT8 immunoreactivity under tau-stress conditions in neuronal models. In addition, CAP1 demonstrated favorable preliminary pharmacokinetic properties, including good aqueous solubility, plasma stability, and measurable membrane permeability. Collectively, these findings establish the first cyclic peptide ligands targeting CAPON and identify CAP1 as a promising scaffold for the modulation of CAPON-dependent neurodegenerative signaling.
Authors: Abdo A; Yuan S; Kuncewicz K; Mo J; Duan H; Gabr MT

Title: Handwriting-based Alzheimer's disease classification on the DARWIN dataset: Repeated nested validation, task-level reduction, and cross-validated explainability.
Abstract: Online handwriting provides a low-burden source of cognitive-motor measurements, but small datasets can yield optimistic results when preprocessing, task selection, or explanation is not separated from evaluation. We evaluated eight classifiers on the DARWIN dataset (174 participants; 25 tasks; 450 predictors) using ten repetitions of 5-outer/3-inner-fold nested stratified cross-validation. All preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and calibration were restricted to outer training data. We added a training-derived operating point, fully nested seven-task selection, cross-model subset transfer, foldwise SHAP analysis, and an all-feature SHAP sensitivity analysis. Random Forest had the highest descriptive ROC-AUC (0.938 ± 0.033 across 50 held-out folds). The Friedman omnibus test indicated model differences (p < 0.001), but no one of 28 paired comparisons remained significant after Holm correction. Training-derived thresholds (median 0.461) yielded held-out sensitivity 0.869 and specificity 0.831; these are exploratory operating characteristics, not a clinical cutoff. Nested seven-task selection achieved AUC 0.916 ± 0.037, compared with 0.956 ± 0.030 for all 25 tasks, and selected subsets were unstable (mean Jaccard 0.195). Cross-validated SHAP emphasized temporal variables, although an all-450-feature sensitivity analysis showed that individual ranks depend partly on ANOVA preselection. The study contributes an integrated, leakage-controlled evaluation rather than a new classifier or a validated diagnostic instrument; external prospective validation remains necessary.
Authors: Fatima T; Lashari TA; Moetesum M; Lashari SA

Title: Targeting the P2X7 receptor in Alzheimer's disease: mechanistic insights and emerging therapeutic strategies.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide and is characterized by progressive cognitive decline, amyloid-β deposition, tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and neuronal loss. Current therapies provide only limited symptomatic benefit, and although anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies have demonstrated disease-modifying potential in selected patients, additional disease-modifying targets are still needed. The purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R), an ATP-gated ion channel predominantly expressed on microglia and astrocytes, has emerged as a key regulator of neuroinflammatory signalling and AD progression. This narrative review summarizes and critically discusses recent preclinical, translational, and clinical evidence published through 2026. Evidence from cellular and animal models, post-mortem human brain analyses, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging studies, and pharmacological investigations was evaluated to assess the role of P2X7R in AD pathogenesis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that extracellular ATP-mediated activation of P2X7R promotes NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β and interleukin-18, thereby sustaining chronic neuroinflammation. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of P2X7R reduced amyloid plaque burden, attenuated tau hyperphosphorylation, improved synaptic function, and ameliorated cognitive deficits in experimental AD models. Human studies further revealed elevated P2X7R expression and increased neuroinflammatory activity associated with AD pathology. Emerging therapeutic approaches include selective P2X7R antagonists, natural-product modulators, RNA-based interventions, nanotechnology-assisted drug delivery systems, and combination therapies targeting multiple pathogenic pathways. P2X7R represents a promising candidate target for disease-modifying therapeutic strategies in AD, based on convergent in vitro, animal-model, human post-mortem, and imaging/biomarker evidence linking ATP-mediated danger signalling to neuroinflammation, amyloid and tau pathology, and neurodegeneration. However, its clinical efficacy in AD remains to be established, as no clinical trial data for P2X7R-targeted therapies in this disease are yet available. Future clinical translation will require improved CNS-penetrant antagonists, enhanced receptor selectivity, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and precision medicine approaches.
Authors: Se ME; Ramalingam A

Title: Plant-derived phytochemicals for Alzheimer's disease: mechanisms of action, experimental evidence, and therapeutic perspectives.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by cholinergic deficits, amyloid-beta accumulation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and synaptic dysfunction, which collectively contribute to cognitive decline and neuronal loss. Conventional pharmacotherapies provide symptomatic relief but largely target single pathological pathways, highlighting the need for multi-targeted approaches. Herbal therapeutics have emerged as promising complementary or alternative interventions, offering multifaceted mechanisms that simultaneously modulate key disease processes. Preclinical studies, including in vitro and animal models, indicate that extracts of medicinal plants, including Bacopa monnieri (aerial parts), Ginkgo biloba (leaves), Curcuma longa (rhizomes), and Withania somnifera (roots), may enhance cognitive function, exert neuroprotective effects, attenuate oxidative stress and inflammation, and modulate amyloid and tau pathology. However, clinical evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and inconclusive, with existing studies reporting variable effects on memory, attention, executive function, and global cognition and generally providing only preliminary evidence of safety and efficacy. This translational gap is further influenced by poor bioavailability and brain delivery of several phytoconstituents, variability in herbal preparations, inadequate standardisation, differences in dosing and study design, and the scarcity of adequately powered, long-term clinical trials. Emerging approaches, including nanotechnology-based delivery systems, rational combinations with conventional therapeutics or complementary herbal agents, and personalised interventions based on genetic and metabolic characteristics, may improve therapeutic precision and clinical translation. Integrating mechanistic insights with experimental and clinical evidence may help identify the most promising herbal candidates while defining their translational limitations. This review synthesises current evidence and future directions, providing a framework for advancing herbal interventions in AD.
Authors: Nimbalkar J; Shinde R

Title: A closer look at LATE: a Case Report on a subtly evolving neurodegenerative disorder.
Abstract: Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) often presents in older adults with a hippocampal-type amnestic syndrome that is clinically indistinguishable from Alzheimer's disease (AD). In the era of anti-amyloid therapies, misdiagnosis carries therapeutic consequences. Single-patient case report. The patient provided written informed consent and all data included in this paper are de-identified. A 71-year-old with isolated episodic memory impairment underwent neuropsychological testing, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) AD biomarkers, and <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET in 2021. Baseline findings showed preserved global cognition, negative AD biomarkers, and mild bilateral medial temporal hypometabolism. Over the subsequent years, episodic memory declined, while daily function and other cognitive domains remained intact. MRI demonstrated bilateral medial temporal atrophy. Repeat CSF examination showed negative AD biomarkers, whereas NfL levels were markedly elevated. On repeat <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET, bilateral medial temporal hypometabolism progressed, while inferolateral temporal metabolism-usually reduced in AD-remained preserved. The slowly progressing isolated amnestic profile, medial temporal-predominant neurodegeneration, high CSF NfL level, and persistently negative AD biomarkers supported the diagnosis of LATE. LATE should be actively considered in elderly patients with a hippocampal-type amnestic syndrome and negative AD biomarkers. This requires a high index of suspicion, but it is increasingly critical to avoid ineffective therapies and to refine clinical trial selection.
Authors: Di Giesi ML; Motolese F; Norata D; Sapio E; Selvaggi SA; Meduri GM; Capone F; Pilato F; Di Lazzaro V
Journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

Title: Expert perspectives on the design and communication of endpoints in Alzheimer's disease clinical trials.
Abstract: Disease-targeted therapies (DTTs) for Alzheimer's disease (AD) represent a major advance, yet challenges remain on how best to interpret and communicate their benefits. As clinical development increasingly targets the earliest stages of AD (before symptoms emerge and early symptomatic AD), there is a need for novel, complementary endpoints and improved communication of treatment benefits. The Global CEO Initiative on Alzheimer's Disease convened a multi-stakeholder working group to develop recommendations for improving the design and communication of endpoints in AD clinical trials. In the near term, communication can be improved by contextualizing treatment effects at the individual level, including framing benefits in terms of responder analyses and "time saved" over defined timeframes. In parallel, continued development of complementary endpoints is needed to enable more sensitive, scalable, and patient-centered measurements aligned with early intervention. These recommendations aim to support stakeholders in evaluating and communicating the meaningful benefits of current and emerging therapies.
Authors: Tariot PN; Dickson SP; Dwyer J; Granda C; Hughes L; Karlawish J; Linz N; Nair KV; Paulsen R; Pawson D; Perneczky R; Schindler SE; Scholler E; Taylor J; Tiede B; Vradenburg G
Journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

Title: Design, Synthesis and Evaluation Donepezil-Based Dual BuChE/FAAH Inhibitors for Alzheimer's Disease Therapy.
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is multifactorial, prompting multi-target therapy. A series of donepezil-based derivatives were designed, synthesized, and evaluated as dual inhibitors of human butyrylcholinesterase (hBuChE) and fatty acid amide hydrolase (hFAAH). Among them, lead G15 displayed potent and balanced inhibition with IC50 values of 2.44 μM and 0.17 μM, respectively, and favorable selectivity over carboxylesterases CES1/2 (SI 14.4 and 8.4). G15 not only acted as a time-dependent, mixed-type hFAAH inhibitor and a pseudo-irreversible hBuChE inhibitor, but also exhibited good drug-like properties, including high BBB permeability and oral bioavailability (108%). Moreover, G15 chelated Zn2+, protected PC12 cells from oxidative stress, and promoted microglial M1 → M2 polarization. In an Aβ1-42-induced mouse model, G15 significantly reversed cognitive deficits, outperforming donepezil. Therefore, G15 is poised for further development as a promising multi-target candidate for AD therapy.
Authors: Liu X; Wu Y; Ding Y; Hu S; Hou H; Zong Y; Zhang Z; Tang W

Title: "Morphological, Functional, and Molecular Progression of Blood-Brain Barrier Dysfunction in Alzheimer's Disease".
Abstract: Blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction is increasingly recognized as an early pathological event in sporadic Alzheimer's disease (AD), which represents over 95% of cases. Vascular risk factors and cerebral insulin resistance are considered potential contributors to its initiation. This review synthesizes evidence available through March 2026 on the temporal progression of morphological, functional, and molecular BBB alterations in AD patients and experimental models. This review emphasizes the proposed role of BBB disruption in perpetuating neurodegeneration through feedback loops involving pericyte damage, hypoxia, perivascular inflammation, and dysregulation of amyloid-β transport systems. By integrating data from neuroimaging, fluid biomarkers, and post-mortem studies, available evidence suggests that BBB alterations can be detected from preclinical stages, most consistently in the hippocampus, and may exhibit sex-specific differences. The review compares findings from familial transgenic models with the more limited characterization available in sporadic AD models (notably the intracerebroventricular streptozotocin model), and highlights key knowledge gaps regarding temporal dynamics. This synthesis supports further exploration of strategies to preserve BBB integrity. An integrated vascular approach may usefully complement current amyloid- and tau-centered therapies, particularly in sporadic AD.
Authors: León-Arcia K; Martínez-Orozco H; Guerra-Crespo M; Díaz-Miranda SY; Soto-Rojas LO

Title: Association Between Plasma N-Terminal Tau, Cognitive Decline, and Neurodegeneration in the ADNI Cohort.
Abstract: Blood-based biomarkers offer a cost-effective, minimally invasive alternative to neuroimaging and CSF biomarkers. Newly developed fluid biomarkers, including the N-terminal tau fragment (NT1), show promise for identifying individuals at risk for Alzheimer disease (AD) and for monitoring disease progression. Here, we determine whether NT1 levels are associated with key clinical and biomarker measures in a large, well-characterized cohort. Participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort with available plasma NT1, β-amyloid (Aβ)-PET, MRI, and clinical measures (Clinical Dementia Rating) were included in this observational study. NT1 was measured using the Quanterix Simoa HD-X platform. PET, MRI, clinical, and other plasma measures were obtained using established ADNI procedures. A subset also had NULISA-based plasma measures of amyloid and tau and tau-PET assessed. Linear regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between NT1 and clinical or biomarker measures, adjusting for relevant covariates. Multivariable-adjusted Cox regression was performed to evaluate the association between baseline NT1 levels and risk of clinically diagnosed mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD. Mediation analysis was conducted to examine whether hippocampal atrophy mediates the relationship between NT1 and memory decline. Spearman correlations were used to examine continuous relationships between plasma NT1 and continuous fluid and neuroimaging markers. A total of 755 participants (mean age: 72.9 [7.0], female: 375 [50%]) were included in the study. Plasma NT1 levels were elevated in MCI/AD individuals (BMCI/AD [SE] = 0.09 [0.022], p = 1.98 × 10-4) and were cross-sectionally associated with worse memory performance (B [SE] = -0.25 [0.09], p = 0.005). Aβ moderated the association between elevated NT1 and greater cognitive decline across multiple domains (memory: B [SE] = -0.17 [0.074], p = 0.022; executive function: B [SE] = -0.24 [0.082], p = 0.004; language: B [SE] = -0.21 [0.075], p = 0.006). NT1 levels were negatively associated with hippocampal volume (B [SE] = -264.49 [125.99], p = 0.036) and predicted longitudinal atrophy (B [SE] = -42.00 [16.90], p = 0.013). Accelerated hippocampal atrophy largely mediated the association between higher baseline NT1 level and greater memory decline (B [95% CI]indirect effect = -0.082 [-0.135 to -0.03], p = 0.003, B [95% CI]proportion mediated = 70.1% [32.6%-155.3%], p = 0.004). Higher NT1 levels were associated with higher levels of plasma biomarkers, including NULISA-based brain-derived (BD) plasma pTau (BD-pTau181, BD-pTau217, BD-pTau231: p's < 5.01 × 10-6) and Simoa-Based pTau181 (p < 4.51 × 10-15) and neurofilament light chain (p < 5.34 × 10-7). Plasma NT1 may be useful in assessing amyloid-dependent cognitive decline and neurodegeneration.
Authors: Rao Y; Liu L; Ostaszewski BL; Anderson AK; Pinilla V; Shirzadi Z; Laho EM; Stern AM; Yau WW; Yang HS; Buckley RF; Ashton NJ; Denkinger MN; Sperling RA; Selkoe DJ; Chhatwal JP; Schultz SA
